subject: ss
title: Social Studies Practices: Maps, Data, Sources, and Bias
objectives: You will read maps shown as grids or tables, using direction, a key, and a scale to locate places and measure distances.
You will interpret bar graphs, line graphs, circle graphs, and tables, and choose only the conclusions the data actually support.
You will distinguish primary sources from secondary sources and judge what each kind of source can and cannot prove.
You will identify bias, propaganda techniques, fact versus opinion, and point of view in documents, posters, ads, and cartoons described in words.
You will identify cause-and-effect relationships and avoid treating a sequence or a correlation as proof of cause.

slides.title: Social Studies Practices: Maps, Data, Sources, and Bias
slides.board:
Week 9 Social Studies: Maps, Data, Sources, and Bias

Today you will:

  • Read grid maps: direction, key, and scale
  • Read bar, line, and circle graphs and tables, and pick only supported conclusions
  • Tell primary from secondary sources and say what each can prove
  • Spot bias, propaganda, fact vs. opinion, and point of view
  • Separate cause and effect from “happened after”

Plan: Warm-up → five skills → we do it together → you do it → GED questions

notes.say: This week is different from the last eight. Instead of one topic, we practice the reading skills that the GED Social Studies test uses on every topic: maps, charts, sources, bias, and cause and effect. Almost every question on the test hands you something to read or look at first, and the answer is built from that stimulus. If you master these five skills, you can answer questions about events you have never studied, because the evidence is right in front of you.
ask: When you see a chart in the news or on social media, what do you look at first? (Expected: any honest answer. Use it to set up the habit for today: title, labels, and units before any numbers.)

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 8 Review
slides.board:
Answer each one.

  1. In one day, a worker in Marlo makes 6 bikes or 12 chairs. A worker in Nessa makes 2 bikes or 8 chairs. Which country has the comparative advantage in bikes?
  2. On a grid where each line is 1°, a city is 4 lines above the equator and 7 lines left of the prime meridian. Write its coordinates.
  3. A drought ruins a family’s farm, so they move to a city with factory jobs. Name the push factor and the pull factor.
  4. A country puts a 20% tariff on imported steel. Who is helped, and who pays more?
steps: Marlo. One bike costs Marlo 12 ÷ 6 = 2 chairs. One bike costs Nessa 8 ÷ 2 = 4 chairs. Marlo gives up less.
4°N, 7°W. Above the equator is north, left of the prime meridian is west, and latitude is written first.
Push: the drought that ruined the farm. Pull: the factory jobs in the city.
Helped: steel makers at home, who face less foreign competition. Pays more: buyers of steel, such as builders and carmakers, and in the end their customers.

notes.say: These four questions review last week: comparative advantage, latitude and longitude, push and pull factors, and tariffs. Give the student about four minutes, then have them tell you each answer and the reason before you reveal it. Notice that question 2 is already a map skill; today we build on it with grid maps, keys, and scales.
ask: For question 1, who has the absolute advantage in bikes? (Expected: Marlo, which makes more bikes, 6 versus 2. Here the same country has both, but that is not always true.)
For question 3, how do you tell push from pull? (Expected: push is about the old place, pull is about the new place)
notes.answer: 1. Marlo (a bike costs 2 chairs there versus 4 in Nessa). 2. 4°N, 7°W. 3. Push: drought; pull: factory jobs. 4. Domestic steel makers are helped; steel buyers and their customers pay more.
notes.watch: On question 1, students often divide the wrong way (bikes ÷ chairs) and then pick the larger number. Have them say the sentence: “To make one bike, I give up ___ chairs.” On question 2, watch for 7°W, 4°N: latitude always comes first.

slides.title: Reading a Map: Title, North, Key, Scale
slides.board:
Find four things first: Title · North · Key · Scale

Pine Valley (fictional). North is at the top. Each square is 2 miles.

1 (west)234 (east)
A (north)ForestPine ValleyFarmlandLake Ross
BForestHighway 5Oak SpringsFarmland
C (south)QuarryFarmlandFarmlandDunmore

notes.say: Before you answer any map question, find the title, which way is north, the key, and the scale. The key (or legend) tells you what symbols and labels mean, and the scale tells you how far one unit on the map is in real life. On this course’s tests, many maps are shown as grids: rows with letters, columns with numbers. With north at the top, a lower row is farther south and a higher column number is farther east. For direction, compare rows first (north or south), then columns (east or west), and combine them. For distance, count the squares you move, center to center, and multiply by the scale.
ask: Which square is farthest northeast on this map? (Expected: A4, Lake Ross: top row, highest column)
What does the scale tell you here? (Expected: each square is 2 miles on a side)
notes.watch: Students often count squares the way they count fence posts: B2, B3, B4 is “three squares,” but you only move two. Have them put a finger on the start square and count each step.

slides.title: Worked Example: Direction and Distance
slides.board:
Use the Pine Valley map.

  1. In which direction is Dunmore (C4) from Pine Valley (A2)?
  2. How far is Lake Ross (A4) from Pine Valley (A2), center to center?
  3. In which direction is Pine Valley from Dunmore?
steps: Start at the “from” place. Question 1 starts at Pine Valley, A2.
Rows: A to C moves down the map: south. Columns: 2 to 4 moves right: east. Combine: southeast.
Distance: both are in row A. Column 2 to column 4 is 4 − 2 = 2 squares. 2 × 2 miles = 4 miles.
Reverse trip: start at Dunmore (C4). C to A is north; 4 to 2 is west. Pine Valley is northwest of Dunmore, the exact opposite of question 1.

notes.say: Model the method out loud, and stress the word from. “Where is A from B?” means: stand at B and travel to A. That one word decides the answer, and the GED loves to offer the reverse direction as a trap. Then show that the distance is the number of squares you move, multiplied by the scale.
ask: If each square were 5 miles instead of 2, how far would Lake Ross be from Pine Valley? (Expected: 2 × 5 = 10 miles)
notes.watch: If the student says “northwest” for question 1, they started at Dunmore. Ask: “Where are you standing when you start?”

slides.title: We Do: Grid Map Practice
slides.board:
A grid map has north at the top. Each square is 10 miles. Fairview is in B1, Kent is in B4, and Millton is in D1.

  1. How far apart are Fairview and Kent, center to center?
  2. In which direction is Kent from Millton?
  3. How far is Millton from Fairview?
steps: 30 miles. Same row (B). Column 1 to column 4 is 3 squares. 3 × 10 = 30.
Northeast. Start at Millton (D1). D to B is up the map (north); 1 to 4 is right (east).
20 miles. Same column (1). Row B to row D is 2 squares. 2 × 10 = 20.

notes.say: Now we do it together. Have the student sketch a quick grid on paper, rows A to D down the side and columns 1 to 4 across the top, and place the three towns. Ask them to name the start square before every direction question. Reveal each answer only after they commit.
ask: For number 2, which town do you start at? (Expected: Millton, because the question says “from Millton”)
For number 1, why is it not 40 miles? (Expected: you move 3 squares, not 4; you do not count the square you start in)
notes.watch: If the student answers “southwest” for number 2, they described Millton from Kent. Have them say the question back: “Kent, from Millton.”

slides.title: Charts, Graphs, and Tables
slides.board:
DisplayBest for
Bar graphComparing amounts across groups
Line graphChange over time
Circle (pie) graphParts of one whole (adds to 100%)
TableExact values

Read first: title → labels → units → source.
A percent is a share, not a count.
A supported conclusion uses only what the data show.

notes.say: Before reading a single number, read the title, the axis labels, the units, and the source line. Ask: what is being measured, in what units, for what group, and over what time? A bar graph compares groups, a line graph shows change over time, a circle graph shows how one whole is divided, and a table gives exact numbers. Two traps cause most wrong answers on data questions. First, a percent is a share of a total, so a bigger percent is not always a bigger number of people. Second, a chart shows what happened, not why; any answer that says “caused” needs more evidence than the chart gives.
ask: A chart shows the share of a city’s budget spent on parks each year. Which display would show the trend best? (Expected: a line graph, because it is change over time)
What must the slices of a circle graph add up to? (Expected: 100 percent of one whole)
notes.watch: Students skip the units. Point out that “millions,” “percent,” and “thousands of dollars” change every answer. Make them say the units aloud before reading any value.

slides.title: Worked Example: What Does the Table Support?
slides.board:
YearU.S. population (census count)
190076.2 million
1950151.3 million
2000281.4 million
2020331.4 million

Which conclusion is supported?
(a) The population roughly doubled from 1900 to 1950.
(b) Large families caused most of the growth after 1950.
(c) The population grew faster from 2000 to 2020 than from 1950 to 2000.
steps: Check (a): 76.2 × 2 = 152.4. The 1950 count, 151.3 million, is very close. Supported.
Check (b): The table gives totals only. It never says why the population grew. Not supported, even if it might be true.

Check (c): 2000 to 2020: 331.4 − 281.4 = 50.0 million in 20 years. 1950 to 2000: 281.4 − 151.3 = 130.1 million in 50 years, or about 26 million per 10 years versus 25 million per 10 years. Not faster. Not supported.
Answer: (a). It is the only statement you can prove with these four numbers.

notes.say: These are real census counts, rounded. Show the student how to test each answer against the numbers, out loud. Answer (b) is the classic GED trap: it sounds reasonable, but the table cannot show causes. Answer (c) needs a careful comparison, because the two periods are different lengths, so we compare growth per ten years.
ask: By how many millions did the population grow from 2000 to 2020? (Expected: 331.4 − 281.4 = 50.0 million)
What kind of source would you need to support (b)? (Expected: data on births, family size, and immigration, not just totals)
notes.watch: If the student picks (c) because 50 million “feels big,” ask them to compare equal time spans. Twenty years is not fifty years.

slides.title: Worked Example: Percent Is Not a Count
slides.board:
Two fictional towns. The graph shows the share of workers who ride the bus to work.

TownTotal workers
Ashby10,000
Brill5,000

Brill has the higher percent. Does Brill have more bus riders?

figure.title: Workers Who Ride the Bus to Work

steps: Read the units: the graph shows percent of workers, not numbers of riders.
Ashby: 20% of 10,000 = 0.20 × 10,000 = 2,000 riders.
Brill: 30% of 5,000 = 0.30 × 5,000 = 1,500 riders.
Answer: No. Brill has the larger share, but Ashby has 500 more riders. To turn a percent into a count, you need the total.

notes.say: This is the most common data trap on the test. A percent tells you the share of a group, and the same percent of a bigger group is a bigger number. Walk through both multiplications, then ask: if the graph did not give the totals, could we say which town had more riders? We could not. When an answer choice talks about “more people” and the chart only shows percents, look for the totals before you agree.
ask: If the table were missing, which statement could you still make? (Expected: a larger share of Brill’s workers ride the bus)
notes.watch: Students read a taller bar as “more people.” Point to the y-axis label every time: “percent of what?”

slides.title: We Do: Read the Line Graph
slides.board:
Brookside County is fictional. The graph shows the number of farms in the county.

  1. How many fewer farms were there in 2020 than in 1980?
  2. In which 10-year period did the number fall the most?
  3. Does the graph show why the number of farms fell?
steps: 440 fewer. 1,200 − 760 = 440.
A tie: 1980–1990 and 1990–2000, each a drop of 150 (1,200 − 1,050 and 1,050 − 900). 2000–2010 fell 80 and 2010–2020 fell 60.

No. The graph shows what happened (fewer farms each decade), not why. Larger farms buying smaller ones, rising land prices, or families leaving farming are possible reasons, but this graph cannot tell us which.

notes.say: Read the title, the axis labels, and the units together before you answer. Then have the student compute each decade’s change on paper. Number 2 is a good lesson in reading carefully: the steepest drops are in the first two decades, and the line flattens after 2000. Number 3 sets up our last skill of the day, cause and effect.
ask: What is the overall trend? (Expected: the number of farms fell every decade, but more slowly after 2000)
notes.answer: 1. 440 fewer farms. 2. 1980–1990 and 1990–2000 tie, each −150. 3. No; the graph shows the change, not its cause.
notes.watch: On number 1, some students subtract neighboring points only (1,200 − 1,050 = 150). Ask: “Which two years does the question name?”

slides.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
slides.board:
PrimarySecondary
Who made it?A participant or witnessSomeone who studied it later
When?At or near the timeAfter the fact
ExamplesLetters, diaries, speeches, laws, photos, posters, original dataTextbooks, encyclopedias, documentaries, most history books
StrengthFirst-hand; shows how people thought thenBroader view; context
CautionOne creator’s point of viewThe author’s interpretation

notes.say: A primary source was created by someone who took part in or witnessed an event, at or near the time. A secondary source describes or interprets the event afterward, usually using primary sources. The type depends on who made it and when, not on the topic and not on whether it is true. Neither type is automatically more accurate: a speech or poster was often made to persuade, and a textbook reflects its author’s choices. A good historian uses both and asks what each one can and cannot prove.
ask: Is a primary source always more trustworthy than a secondary source? (Expected: No. It shows one person’s view and may be biased or mistaken)
Is a 2010 documentary that shows old film clips primary or secondary? (Expected: secondary as a whole; it was made later to interpret the past)
notes.watch: Students think “old” means primary. A 1920 history book about the Civil War is old, but it is secondary. Ask: “Was the creator there at the time?”

slides.title: Worked Example: The Gettysburg Address
slides.board:
On November 19, 1863, during the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln spoke at the dedication of a soldiers’ cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania:

“Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.”

Primary or secondary? What is it good evidence of?
steps: Who and when? Lincoln, a leader in the war, speaking during the war. That makes it a primary source.
Good evidence of: how Lincoln explained the purpose of the war to the public in 1863.
Not good evidence of: how every American felt about the war, or what happened in the battle itself.
Decode: a score is 20. 4 × 20 + 7 = 87 years. 1863 − 87 = 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence and its claim that “all men are created equal.”

notes.say: Classify the source, then go one step further: what can this source prove, and what can it not prove? That second question is where GED source items live. A speech shows what the speaker wanted listeners to believe. It does not show what the listeners actually believed. Finish with the arithmetic, because it shows Lincoln deliberately tying the war to the founding ideals.
ask: Would a 2015 book that analyzes the speech be primary or secondary? (Expected: secondary; it was written long afterward to interpret the speech)
notes.watch: If the student says “secondary, because Lincoln was not fighting,” remind them that a participant does not have to be a soldier. The president leading the war was a participant.

slides.title: We Do: Primary or Secondary?
slides.board:
1. A soldier’s letter home, written in 1944
  2. A 1995 documentary about D-Day
  3. The text of the Nineteenth Amendment (1920)
  4. A biography of Susan B. Anthony written in 2005
  5. A newspaper report written the day after the 1969 moon landing
steps: 1. Primary: written by a participant during the war.
2. Secondary: made 51 years later to explain the event.
3. Primary: an original government document from the time.
4. Secondary: written long after Anthony’s death (1906) by someone studying her life.
5. Primary: reported at the time by people covering the event as it happened.

notes.say: Read each one aloud and ask the same two questions: who made it, and when? Have the student commit before each reveal. Number 5 is the tricky one: a newspaper report written right after an event counts as a primary source, because it records what was known and said at the time.
ask: Which clue words help most here? (Expected: the dates, compared with the date of the event, and words like letter, text, biography, documentary)
notes.watch: On number 3, students sometimes say a law is “not a source.” Laws, treaties, and court decisions are primary sources: they are the original records of what the government did.

slides.title: Bias and Propaganda
slides.board:
Bias = one-sided. Clues: loaded words, missing facts, only one side quoted, a creator who gains if you agree.

Propaganda = one-sided information spread on purpose to shape opinion.

TechniqueWhat it does
Bandwagon“Everyone is doing it”
Name-callingNegative label
Glittering generalitiesVague feel-good words
TestimonialFamous person endorses
TransferLinks to a respected symbol
Card stackingOnly helpful facts
Plain folks“I’m just like you”
FearDanger unless you act

notes.say: Bias is a one-sided presentation. Look for loaded words such as “reckless” or “heroic,” facts that are left out, only one side being quoted, and a creator who benefits if you agree. Propaganda is one-sided information spread on purpose to shape public opinion. Governments, parties, and businesses all use it, and wartime posters are the classic GED example. Learn these eight techniques by name, because the test may ask you to identify one. Then always ask the bigger question: who made this, and what did they want me to think or do?
ask: A senator’s ad shows her eating at a small-town diner, saying, “I grew up shopping at stores like this.” Which technique? (Expected: plain folks)
What is the difference between testimonial and transfer? (Expected: testimonial uses a real famous person’s endorsement; transfer links the cause to a respected symbol such as the flag)
notes.watch: Students mix up bandwagon and glittering generalities. Bandwagon is about other people doing it; glittering generalities are about vague, positive words.

slides.title: Worked Example: The Uncle Sam Poster
slides.board:
Described poster, 1917: Uncle Sam, a symbol of the United States, wears a top hat with white stars. He stares at the viewer and points his finger straight out. Large letters: “I WANT YOU FOR U.S. ARMY.” Smaller letters: “NEAREST RECRUITING STATION.” Artist: James Montgomery Flagg. More than four million copies were printed in 1917 and 1918, during World War I.

Purpose? Technique? What can it prove?
steps: Purpose: persuade men to enlist. The words point viewers to a recruiting station.
Technique: transfer: the respect people feel for their country (Uncle Sam) is linked to joining the army. The pointing finger and “YOU” make it a direct personal appeal.
Good evidence of: how the government tried to build support for the war.
Not good evidence of: how many men enlisted because of it, or how the public really felt about the war.

notes.say: On the GED, posters and cartoons are often described in words. Read the description slowly and notice three things: who or what is shown, any words printed on the image, and the date. Then name the purpose and the technique. The last two steps are the ones students forget: a persuasive poster is excellent evidence of what its makers wanted, and weak evidence of what people actually did.
ask: Why is this not a testimonial? (Expected: Uncle Sam is a symbol, not a real famous person endorsing the army)
notes.watch: Some students say the poster “proves people supported the war.” Ask: “Does the poster tell us anything about the people who saw it, or only about the people who made it?”

slides.title: Fact, Opinion, and Point of View
slides.board:
Fact: can be checked and proven true or false.
Opinion: a belief or judgment. Signal words: should, best, worst, unfair, wise, disgraceful, I believe.
Point of view: where a person stands shapes what they notice and how they describe it.

“The fare rose to $2.00 in March.” → fact
“The $2.00 fare is far too high.” → opinion (a number does not make it a fact)

notes.say: A fact can be checked in records, measurements, or documents. An opinion is a judgment that people can reasonably disagree about, even when it contains a number. Underline the judgment words: too high, best, unfair, should. Point of view is the position from which a person sees an event. A factory owner and a striking worker can describe the same strike in completely different words, and both accounts can be honest primary sources. Their point of view decides which facts they include and which words they choose.
ask: Fact or opinion: “The council should have waited until next year to raise the fare.” (Expected: opinion; “should” signals a recommendation)

Can a statement be false and still be a fact statement? (Expected: yes; “The fare rose to $3.00” is checkable, and checking shows it is false. On the GED, “fact” means it can be proven true or false.)
notes.watch: Students label every sentence with a number as a fact. Write “The $42,000 cost is a waste” and ask them to underline the judgment.

slides.title: Worked Example: Two Accounts of One Fare Increase
slides.board:
Transit director: “The board voted 5 to 2 to raise the fare from $1.50 to $2.00. Fuel costs rose 30 percent this year. This modest change keeps every route running.”

Bus rider: “I ride twice a day, so the new fare costs me $20 more each month. The board did not hold a single evening hearing. This increase is unfair to working families.”
steps: Facts both could check: the 5–2 vote, the fares, the 30 percent fuel increase, the $20 a month (2 rides × $0.50 × 20 workdays), whether there was an evening hearing.
Opinions: “modest change” (director) and “unfair to working families” (rider).
Point of view: the director stresses costs and keeping routes running; the rider stresses the cost to riders and the missing hearing. Each includes the facts that support their side.
Conclusion: both accounts are primary sources, and both are one-sided. Together they give a fuller picture.

notes.say: Sort each account into facts and opinions, then ask why the two people chose different facts. That is point of view. Show the student that the rider’s $20 is a checkable fact: 50 cents more per ride, two rides a day, about 20 workdays a month. Neither writer is lying; each is selecting.
ask: Which phrase shows the director’s point of view most clearly? (Expected: “modest change,” a judgment that downplays the increase)
notes.watch: If a student calls the rider “biased” and the director “neutral,” point out that “modest” is just as much a judgment as “unfair.”

slides.title: We Do: Name the Technique
slides.board:
1. “Over two million families have already switched to Brightline Power. Don’t be left behind!”
  2. “Only a fool would support Mayor Diaz’s reckless plan.”
  3. “Senator Park stands for freedom, family, and a brighter tomorrow.”
  4. “If Measure 4 fails, criminals will roam our streets. Vote yes.”
steps: 1. Bandwagon: everyone else is doing it.
2. Name-calling: “fool” and “reckless” attach negative labels instead of giving reasons.
3. Glittering generalities: feel-good words with no specific plans.
4. Fear: warns of danger unless you act.

notes.say: Read each one aloud. Ask the student to name the technique and then point to the words that prove it. For each, ask the follow-up: what information is missing? For example, number 3 never says what Park would actually do. Reveal after they commit.
ask: What does number 2 leave out? (Expected: any actual reason the plan is bad)
Is the “two million families” in number 1 a fact or an opinion? (Expected: a fact claim, because it can be checked, even though the ad uses it for bandwagon)
notes.watch: Students often call number 2 “fear.” Ask: “Is it warning of danger, or attacking a person with a label?”

slides.title: Cause, Effect, and Correlation
slides.board:
Cause = why it happened. Effect = what happened as a result.
Signal words: because, led to, as a result, therefore, due to.

Chains: an effect often becomes the next cause.
Drought → crops die → families cannot pay debts → families move

After ≠ because of. Two things changing together (correlation) is not proof that one caused the other.

notes.say: A cause makes something happen; an effect is the result. Many history questions ask you to put a chain of causes and effects in order, and the signal words tell you the direction. The biggest trap on data questions is treating a sequence or a correlation as proof. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer, but ice cream does not cause sunburn; hot, sunny weather drives both. To test a cause, look for evidence that rules out other explanations, such as a comparison with a similar place where the supposed cause did not happen.
ask: Crime fell the year after a town installed brighter streetlights. Does that prove the lights caused the drop? (Expected: no; other changes could explain it)
What evidence would help test that claim? (Expected: crime trends in similar towns that did not add lights over the same years)
notes.watch: On multiple choice, answers containing “caused,” “proves,” or “because of” are often traps on data questions. Teach the student to ask: “Does the evidence show why, or only what?”

slides.title: Worked Example: Did the Factory Do It?
slides.board:
Grant County (fictional) opened a large factory in 2014. A student says, “The factory cut unemployment in half.”

Is the claim supported by the graph? What would test it?
steps: What the graph shows: the rate fell from 8% in 2012 to 4% in 2018. That is half.
Timing problem: the rate was already falling before 2014 (8% to 7%). Something else was already at work.
What the graph does not show: why the rate fell. A national recovery or people leaving the workforce could also explain it.
Better evidence: how many county residents the factory hired, and unemployment in similar counties with no new factory over the same years. Conclusion: the claim is not supported by the graph alone.

notes.say: This is the reasoning the GED wants on every cause question. First, state what the data show. Second, check the timing: a cause must come before its effect, and here the drop began before the factory opened. Third, name other possible causes. Fourth, name the evidence that would actually test the claim. Those four moves will get you through almost any “Which conclusion is supported” question.
ask: Name one fact that would make the claim stronger. (Expected: the factory hired many local unemployed workers, or similar counties without a factory did not see the same drop)
notes.watch: Students often decide the claim is “true” or “false.” The GED asks whether it is supported. The factory may have helped; this graph just cannot prove it.

slides.title: You Do 1: Maps and Data
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. On a grid map with north at the top, Town X is in D1 and Town Y is in A1. In which direction is Town Y from Town X?
  2. Each square is 4 miles. Two towns in the same row are 5 columns apart. How far apart are they, center to center?
  3. A circle graph shows that 25% of a $40 million city budget goes to roads. How many dollars is that?
  4. A graph shows the share of workers who bike to work rose from 2% to 4%. Can you conclude that more people bike?
steps: 1. North. 2. 20 miles (5 × 4). 3. $10 million (0.25 × 40). 4. Not by itself. A percent is a share; if the total number of workers fell enough, the count could be the same or lower. You need the totals.

notes.say: Start a four-minute timer and stay quiet. When time is up, have the student tell you all four answers and explain number 4 in their own words before you reveal. Number 4 is the one to listen for: the student should mention the total.
ask: For number 4, what extra information would let you decide? (Expected: the total number of workers in each year)
notes.answer: 1. North. 2. 20 miles. 3. $10 million. 4. No; percents alone do not show counts.

slides.title: You Do 2: Sources, Facts, and Opinions
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. Primary or secondary: a diary kept by a nurse during World War II?
  2. Primary or secondary: an encyclopedia article on the causes of World War I?
  3. Fact or opinion: “The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920.”
  4. Fact or opinion: “The new stadium is the best thing ever to happen to our city.”
steps: 1. Primary (a witness, at the time). 2. Secondary (written later to explain). 3. Fact (checkable in records). 4. Opinion (“best thing ever” is a judgment).

notes.say: Three minutes, on their own. When time is up, ask for each answer and the clue that proves it. Praise reasons, not just labels: “The nurse was there, at the time, so primary.”
ask: What word proves number 4 is an opinion? (Expected: “best”)

slides.title: You Do 3: Bias and Cause
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. “Join the millions of Americans who have already signed up!” Name the technique.
  2. A TV ad shows a famous quarterback saying, “This is the only sports drink I trust.” Name the technique.
  3. Put these in cause-and-effect order: soil blows away in dust storms; farmers plow up deep-rooted grasses; a long drought dries the bare soil.
  4. After a city added bike lanes, cycling injuries fell. Does that prove the lanes caused the drop?
steps: 1. Bandwagon. 2. Testimonial. 3. Grasses plowed up → drought dries the bare soil → soil blows away. 4. No. It came after, but other changes (fewer riders, a new helmet law, a mild winter) could explain it. Compare with similar cities that did not add lanes.

notes.say: Four minutes, on their own. For number 3, have the student say each link with “which led to.” For number 4, listen for a specific other explanation or a specific comparison, not just “maybe not.”
ask: For number 3, why must the plowing come before the dust storms? (Expected: the grass roots held the soil; once they were gone, the dry soil could blow away)
notes.answer: 1. Bandwagon. 2. Testimonial. 3. Plowing → drought → dust storms. 4. No; a correlation in time is not proof.

slides.title: GED Question 1: What Do the Data Support?
slides.board:
Elm County (fictional): households with internet at home — 2010: 70% · 2015: 78% · 2020: 88% · 2024: 92%

Which conclusion is supported by the data?

A. The number of households with internet more than doubled from 2010 to 2024.
B. The share of households with home internet rose in every period shown.
C. Falling prices caused more households to get internet.
D. By 2024, every household in Elm County had internet at home.
steps: Eliminate A. The data are percents, not counts, and 70% to 92% is not even a doubling of the share. Without the number of households, we cannot say how the count changed.
Eliminate C. Nothing in the data mentions prices. The data show what changed, not why.
Eliminate D. 92% is not 100%. About 8% of households still lacked home internet.
Answer B. 70 → 78 → 88 → 92: each value is higher than the one before it.

notes.say: Have the student choose before you reveal anything, then eliminate out loud with a reason for each. This question uses all three classic data traps: a percent treated as a count, a cause the data cannot show, and an answer that goes too far. Notice that the right answer is plain and modest. On data questions, the supported answer usually is.
ask: By how many percentage points did the share rise from 2010 to 2024? (Expected: 92 − 70 = 22 percentage points)
notes.answer: B. The share rose in every period shown.
notes.watch: Students who choose C are using real-world knowledge. Ask: “Where in the data are prices?”

slides.title: GED Question 2: Bias in a Source
slides.board:
In 1912, a newspaper owned by the Riverside Lumber Company printed this editorial (fictional):

“The so-called reformers pushing a state forest law are dreamers who know nothing of honest work. Our mills employ 900 local men. This law would put every one of them on the street.”

Which statement best describes the editorial?

A. It is unbiased because it gives an exact number of workers.
B. It is a secondary source because a newspaper printed it.
C. It shows only the costs of the law and uses name-calling, which serves the owner’s business.
D. It proves that the forest law would have closed the mills.
steps: Eliminate A. One checkable number does not make a source unbiased. The editorial still uses loaded words and tells only one side.
Eliminate B. It was written at the time by people with a stake in the law, so it is a primary source. Who printed it does not make it secondary.
Eliminate D. “Would put every one of them on the street” is a prediction and an opinion, not proof.
Answer C. “Dreamers who know nothing of honest work” is name-calling, it gives no benefits of the law, and the paper’s owner is the lumber company that gains if readers oppose it.

notes.say: Start with the source line: who owned the paper? A lumber company writing about a forest law has something to gain. Then find the loaded words and ask what is missing: the editorial never says what the law would protect or why reformers want it. That combination, a creator with a stake plus one-sided content, is the definition of bias.
ask: What information would a fair account include? (Expected: what the law would actually require and why supporters want it)
notes.answer: C. It shows only the costs and uses name-calling, which serves the owner’s business.
notes.watch: Students who choose D are taking the writer’s prediction as fact. Ask: “Has this happened, or is the writer saying it will?”

slides.title: GED Strategy: Question the Stimulus
slides.board:
1. Spend 20 seconds on the stimulus: title, source line, labels, units, date.
  2. Ask four questions: Who made it? When? Why? What does it actually show?
  3. Read the question, then find the exact words or numbers that answer it.
  4. Cross out answers that claim more than the stimulus shows: caused, proves, all, every, always.
  5. Check units: percent or count? millions or thousands?

Pace: about 2 minutes per question on our practice tests.

notes.say: This is the habit that ties today together. Every stimulus has a creator, a date, a purpose, and limits. If the student asks the four questions before reading the answer choices, the traps become easy to see: a percent treated as a count, a cause the chart cannot show, a poster taken as proof of what people felt. Practice the 20-second scan on every item this week.
ask: What are the four questions? (Expected: Who made it? When? Why? What does it actually show?)
notes.watch: Fast readers jump straight to the answer choices and get pulled toward the one that sounds most interesting. Make them point to the proof before they click.

slides.title: Recap and Next Steps
slides.board:
• Maps: title, north, key, scale. “From B” means start at B. Distance = squares moved × scale.
  • Data: read title, labels, units first. A percent is a share, not a count. Supported means provable from the data.
  • Sources: primary = there, at the time; secondary = later interpretation. Ask what each can prove.
  • Bias: loaded words, missing facts, a creator who gains. Name the technique.
  • Cause: after ≠ because of; correlation is not proof.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice (Set A) → Exit Check

notes.say: Have the student state each takeaway in their own words. Then set up the week: the Student Lesson reviews each skill with a check on every screen, the Practice has 15 GED-style questions (with a second set if they score under 80 percent), and the Exit Check confirms they are ready for Week 10, our integrated review. These skills will appear on every question of the Practice GED this week, whatever the topic.
ask: Which of the five skills feels weakest right now? (Expected: any answer; point the student to that part of the Student Lesson)

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
On the GED Social Studies test, almost every question starts with something to read or look at: a map, a graph, a speech, a poster, or a short article. The test is less about memorizing facts and more about using what is in front of you. This lesson teaches the skills that work on every topic.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Read maps shown as grids or tables, using direction, a key, and a scale
  • Read bar graphs, line graphs, circle graphs, and tables, and choose only the conclusions the data support
  • Tell primary sources from secondary sources and judge what each can prove
  • Spot bias, propaganda techniques, fact versus opinion, and point of view
  • Identify causes and effects without mistaking “happened after” for “was caused by”

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Answer it before you move on.

screens.title: Question Every Stimulus
screens.html:
A stimulus is whatever the question gives you to read or look at. Before you read the answer choices, spend about 20 seconds asking four questions:

  1. Who made it? A government, a company, a reporter, a historian, someone who was there?
  2. When? At the time of the event, or later?
  3. Why? To inform, to record, or to persuade?
  4. What does it actually show? Only that, and nothing more.

The source line under a document or chart often answers the first three questions for you. For example, “Poster by James Montgomery Flagg, 1917” tells you the creator, the date, and (since it is a poster) a likely purpose: to persuade.

check.prompt: A chart has this source line: “Data from the Northside Parking Company, 2024.” The chart shows that a new parking garage would be “full every day.” Which question should a careful reader ask first?
options: Does the company that made the chart gain if the garage is built?
How many colors were used to draw the bars on the chart?
Is 2024 the most recent year that a chart could show?
Would a circle graph have been easier to read here?
why: The colors are a design choice. They do not tell you whether the data are trustworthy. Ask who made the chart and why.
The date matters, but the bigger issue is the creator. A parking company predicting a full garage has something to gain.
Changing the type of graph would not change who made it or why. Start with “Who made it, and why?”
check.hint: Use the first of the four questions: Who made it?
check.explain: The first question is “Who made it, and why?” A parking company that would profit from a new garage has a reason to show that the garage would be full. That does not make the data false, but it means you should look for other evidence before trusting it. Colors and chart type do not affect whether the source is reliable.

screens.title: Map Basics: Title, North, Key, Scale
screens.html:
Before you answer any map question, find four things:

Title (what place, what topic) • North (usually the top) • Key or legend (what the symbols, colors, or labels mean) • Scale (how far one unit on the map is in real life)

When north is at the top, south is at the bottom, east is to the right, and west is to the left. The in-between directions combine two: northeast is up and to the right, southwest is down and to the left.

Maps come in different kinds. A political map shows borders and cities. A physical map shows landforms such as mountains and rivers. A thematic map shows one topic, such as rainfall or population, often with colors explained in the key.

check.prompt: A thematic map of a state uses colors to show average yearly rainfall. Which part of the map tells you how many inches of rain the dark green areas get?
options: The key, which explains what each color stands for
The scale, which shows how map distance compares to real distance
The compass rose, which shows the directions on the map
The title, which names the state and the topic of the map
why: The scale is for distance, such as “1 inch = 50 miles.” It does not explain what the colors mean.
The compass rose shows north, south, east, and west. It says nothing about rainfall amounts.
The title tells you the map is about rainfall, but not what each color means. That is the job of the key.
check.hint: Which map part explains symbols and colors?
check.explain: The key (legend) explains what the symbols and colors mean, for example “dark green = 40–50 inches.” The title tells you the topic, the scale tells you distance, and the compass rose tells you direction.

screens.title: Grid Maps: Direction and Distance
screens.html:
Many maps on this course’s tests are shown as a grid. Rows have letters and columns have numbers. In the map below, north is at the top, and each square is 2 miles on a side.

Pine Valley (fictional)1 (west)234 (east)
A (north)ForestTown of Pine ValleyFarmlandLake Ross
BForestHighway 5Town of Oak SpringsFarmland
C (south)QuarryFarmlandFarmlandTown of Dunmore

Direction: “Where is A from B?” means start at B. Compare rows (north or south), then columns (east or west), and combine.

Distance: count the squares you move, center to center, then multiply by the scale.

example.prompt: In which direction is Dunmore from Pine Valley, and how far is Lake Ross from Pine Valley?
steps: Start at Pine Valley (A2). Dunmore (C4) is in a lower row (south) and a higher column (east): southeast.
Lake Ross (A4) is in the same row as Pine Valley. Column 2 to column 4 is 2 squares. 2 × 2 miles = 4 miles.
example.answer: Dunmore is southeast of Pine Valley. Lake Ross is 4 miles from Pine Valley.

check.prompt: Using the Pine Valley map, how many miles is it from Oak Springs (B3) to Dunmore (C4) if you travel 1 square south and then 1 square east, along the grid?

mistakes.why: You counted squares (1 + 1 = 2) but did not use the scale. Each square is 2 miles: 2 squares × 2 miles.
You counted 4 squares. The route moves 1 square south and 1 square east, which is 2 squares in all.

check.hint: Count the squares you move, then multiply by the miles per square.
check.explain:
Route: 1 square south (B3 to C3) + 1 square east (C3 to C4) = 2 squares.
Distance: 2 × 2 miles = 4 miles.

Answering 2 counts the squares but forgets that each square is 2 miles.

screens.title: Charts, Graphs, and Tables
screens.html:
Read the title, labels, units, and source before any numbers. Ask: what is being measured, in what units, for what group, and over what time?

DisplayBest forExample
Bar graphComparing amounts across groupsVoter turnout in four counties
Line graphChange over timeA city’s population, 1950–2020
Circle (pie) graphParts of one whole; slices add to 100%How a city budget is divided
TableExact valuesCensus counts by year

A double bar graph puts two years or two groups side by side so you can compare them. Each color is explained in the legend.

check.prompt: A city wants to show what share of its total budget goes to police, schools, roads, and parks this year. The best display is a {{0}}, because {{1}}.

options: circle graph
line graph
table of street names
grid map
why: A line graph shows change over time. This shows one year divided into parts.
Street names have nothing to do with how a budget is divided.
A grid map shows locations, not shares of a budget.

options: the parts make up one whole budget
the budget changes every year
the city has four neighborhoods
it shows exact distances
why: Change over time would call for a line graph, but this shows only this year.
The categories are spending areas, not neighborhoods.
Distances belong on a map, not in a budget display.

check.hint: Is this change over time, or one whole split into parts?
check.explain: A circle graph shows how one whole is divided into parts that add to 100 percent, which is exactly what a budget split is. A line graph would be right for showing how the budget changed over several years.

screens.title: Reading Values and Finding Change
screens.html:
To answer a data question, find the exact values first and write them down. Then calculate.

  • Difference: subtract. If turnout was 42% in one year and 55% in another, the change is 55 − 42 = 13 percentage points.
  • Largest increase: find the change for every category, then compare. Do not just pick the tallest bar.
  • Increase vs. change: a drop of 10 is a big change, but it is not an increase.

The graph below shows how residents of a fictional city, Harbor Point, said they get most of their local news.

figure.title: Main Source of Local News, Harbor Point

example.prompt: Which source had the largest decrease from 2012 to 2024?
steps: TV: 35 − 45 = −10. Newspaper: 12 − 30 = −18. Radio: 8 − 10 = −2.
Websites and apps: 45 − 15 = +30, an increase, so it is not in the running.

check.prompt: Using the graph, by how many percentage points did the share of residents who get local news from websites and apps increase from 2012 to 2024?

mistakes.why: That is the 2024 value only. Find the change: subtract the 2012 value, 45 − 15.
That is the percent increase (30 ÷ 15 = 2 = 200 percent). The question asks for percentage points, so just subtract.
You read the TV bars (45 − 35). Use the websites and apps bars: 45 − 15.

check.hint: Find both bars for websites and apps, then subtract.
check.explain:
2024: 45%. 2012: 15%.
Change: 45 − 15 = 30 percentage points.

Answering 45 reads only one year; the question asks for the change.

screens.title: A Percent Is a Share, Not a Count
screens.html:
A percent tells you a share of a total. A count tells you how many. A bigger percent is not always a bigger number of people, because the totals may be different.

To turn a percent into a count, multiply: count = percent × total. Write the percent as a decimal first (35% = 0.35).

Circle graphs are always about shares of one whole. If the graph gives the total, you can find the dollars or people in any slice.

example.prompt: How many dollars does Maple County spend on roads?
steps: Roads = 25% of $50 million.

check.prompt: Using the circle graph, how many million dollars does Maple County spend on public safety?

mistakes.why: That is the percent, not the dollars. Multiply: 40% of $50 million = 0.40 × 50.
You multiplied 40 × 50 without changing 40% to a decimal. 40% = 0.40, so 0.40 × 50 = 20.

check.hint: Change 40% to a decimal and multiply by the total.
check.explain:
Public safety = 40% of $50 million.
0.40 × 50 = 20, so $20 million.

Answering 40 gives the percent, not the dollar amount.

screens.title: Which Conclusion Is Supported?
screens.html:
A supported conclusion can be proven with the data given, nothing more. Test every answer choice against the numbers. Cross out choices that:

  • claim a cause the data do not show (“because of,” “led to”)
  • treat a percent as a count
  • go too far (“all,” “every,” “always,” “proves”)
  • use information that is not in the stimulus
YearU.S. population (official census count, rounded)
190076.2 million
1950151.3 million
2000281.4 million
2020331.4 million

example.prompt: Supported or not? (a) The population roughly doubled from 1900 to 1950. (b) Large families caused the growth after 1950.
steps: (a) 76.2 × 2 = 152.4, very close to 151.3. Supported.
(b) The table gives totals only, not reasons. Not supported, even if it might be true.
example.answer: Only (a) is supported by the table.

check.prompt: Which statement is supported by the census table?
options: The population grew by about 180 million from 1950 to 2020.
Immigration caused most of the population growth after 2000.
The population has doubled in every 50-year period since 1900.
The population will reach 400 million by about the year 2040.
why: The table shows totals only. It gives no information about immigration or any other cause of growth.
This goes too far. From 1950 to 2000 the population grew from 151.3 to 281.4 million, which is less than double (2 × 151.3 = 302.6).
This is a prediction. The table stops at 2020 and cannot prove what will happen later.
check.hint: Calculate with the numbers. Cross out any choice that gives a cause or a prediction.
check.explain: 331.4 − 151.3 = 180.1 million, so “about 180 million” is supported. The immigration claim names a cause the table does not show, the doubling claim fails for 1950–2000 (151.3 × 2 = 302.6, but the count was 281.4), and the 2040 claim predicts beyond the data.

screens.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
screens.html:
Primary sourceSecondary source
Who made it?Someone who took part in or saw the eventSomeone who studied the event later
When?At or near the timeAfter the fact
ExamplesLetters, diaries, speeches, laws, court decisions, photographs, posters, original data, news reports from the timeTextbooks, encyclopedias, documentaries, most history books, biographies written later

The type depends on who made it and when. It does not depend on the topic, on how old it is today, or on whether it is accurate. A 1920 history of the Civil War is old, but it is secondary, because its author was not there.

check.prompt: Drag each source into the correct category.
choices: A diary kept by a nurse in a field hospital in 1918
A 2012 biography of Frederick Douglass
The text of the Voting Rights Act of 1965
A history of the Civil War published in 1920
A photograph taken at the March on Washington in 1963
check.why: The most common mistake is putting the 1920 history of the Civil War under primary because it is old. Its author wrote decades after the war ended in 1865, so it is secondary.
check.hint: Ask: Was the creator there, at the time?
check.explain:
Primary: the nurse’s 1918 diary (a witness, at the time), the Voting Rights Act (an original government document), and the 1963 photograph (taken at the event).

Secondary: the 2012 biography and the 1920 Civil War history, both written later by people interpreting the past.

screens.title: What Can a Source Prove?
screens.html:
Classifying a source is only the first step. The GED also asks what a source is good evidence of.

  • A speech or poster is strong evidence of what its creator wanted people to believe or do. It is weak evidence of what people actually believed or did.
  • A diary or letter shows one person’s experience and feelings. It does not show what everyone experienced.
  • A secondary source can give context and combine many sources, but it reflects its author’s interpretation.

Neither type is automatically more accurate. Ask: who made this, and what were they in a position to know?

example.prompt: On November 19, 1863, during the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln said at Gettysburg: “Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.” What is the speech good evidence of?
steps: It is a primary source: a war leader, speaking during the war.
It shows how Lincoln explained the meaning of the war to the public. (Four score and seven = 4 × 20 + 7 = 87 years; 1863 − 87 = 1776.)
example.answer: How Lincoln presented the purpose of the war, linking it to the ideals of 1776. It does not show how every American felt.

check.prompt: A historian wants to know how ordinary soldiers felt about the food and living conditions in their camps during the Civil War. Which source would be most useful?
options: Letters that soldiers wrote home from camp during the war
A speech a general gave to Congress urging more funding for supplies
A modern textbook chapter summarizing the major battles of the war
A recruiting poster from 1862 showing smiling soldiers around a campfire
why: A general asking Congress for money had a reason to describe camps in a certain way, and he speaks for himself, not for ordinary soldiers.
A battle summary is secondary and focuses on battles, not on how soldiers felt about daily camp life.
A recruiting poster was made to persuade men to join. Smiling soldiers show what the army wanted viewers to think, not what camp life was like.
check.hint: Who was in a position to know how ordinary soldiers felt, and who had no reason to make camp life look good or bad?
check.explain: Letters written by ordinary soldiers from camp are first-hand accounts of exactly what the historian wants: how soldiers felt about food and living conditions. The recruiting poster is a primary source too, but it was made to persuade, so it shows the army’s message, not soldiers’ real experience.

screens.title: Bias and Loaded Language
screens.html:
Bias is a one-sided presentation that favors one view. Look for these clues:

  • Loaded words that stir strong feelings: calling a crowd “a mob,” a tax “a money grab,” or a plan “reckless.”
  • Missing facts: only the benefits, or only the costs.
  • Only one side quoted.
  • A creator who gains if you agree, such as a company writing about a law that affects it.

A biased source can still contain true facts. Your job is to notice what it chooses to include, what it leaves out, and how it describes things.

check.prompt: The sentences below come from a flyer about a proposed city tax. Click the sentence that uses the most loaded language.
spans: The city council will vote on a 1-cent sales tax on June 3.
The tax would raise about $4 million a year for road repairs.
Council members who back this greedy money grab are robbing hardworking families.
The tax would end after ten years unless voters renew it.
A public hearing will be held at City Hall on May 28.
check.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about raising $4 million a year. It contains a large number, but it reports the amount in neutral words. Loaded language uses emotional labels such as “greedy,” “money grab,” and “robbing.”
check.hint: Look for words chosen to make you angry, not words that give information.
check.explain: The sentence calling the tax a “greedy money grab” and saying council members are “robbing hardworking families” uses words chosen to stir anger, not to inform. The other sentences give checkable details (the date, the amount, the time limit, the hearing) in neutral words.

screens.title: Propaganda Techniques
screens.html:
Propaganda is information, often one-sided, spread on purpose to shape public opinion or behavior. Learn these techniques by name:

TechniqueWhat it doesExample
BandwagonEveryone is doing it“Join the millions who already have!”
Name-callingAttaches a negative label“Only a fool would vote yes.”
Glittering generalitiesVague, feel-good words“Freedom. Progress. Tomorrow.”
TestimonialA famous or trusted person endorsesA star athlete praises a product
TransferLinks a cause to a respected symbolThe flag or Uncle Sam on a poster
Card stackingShows only the facts that help one sideLists benefits, hides costs
Plain folks“I am just like you”A candidate in work boots at a diner
FearWarns of danger unless you act“Act now or lose everything.”

example.prompt: A 1917 poster by James Montgomery Flagg shows Uncle Sam, a symbol of the United States, pointing at the viewer above the words “I WANT YOU FOR U.S. ARMY.” Name the purpose and the technique.
steps: Purpose: the words and “NEAREST RECRUITING STATION” tell men to enlist.
Technique: the respect people feel for their country is linked to joining the army.
example.answer: Purpose: persuade men to enlist. Technique: transfer.

check.prompt: A campaign ad shows a governor in jeans and work boots, eating lunch at a small-town diner. She says, “I grew up shopping on a Main Street just like this one.” The technique is {{0}}. A second ad says, “Nine out of ten voters in your county are backing her. Don’t be left out!” That technique is {{1}}.

options: plain folks
testimonial
transfer
fear
why: Testimonial uses a famous person to endorse someone else. Here the governor is presenting herself, as an ordinary person.
Transfer links a cause to a respected symbol such as the flag. No symbol is used here.
Fear warns of danger. The ad shows nothing threatening.

options: bandwagon
card stacking
name-calling
glittering generalities
why: Card stacking lists only helpful facts about a candidate or plan. This ad is about what other voters are doing.
Name-calling attacks an opponent with a label. The ad does not mention an opponent.
Glittering generalities are vague positive words. This ad is about joining the crowd.

check.hint: First ad: who is she pretending to be? Second ad: what are other people doing?
check.explain: Plain folks: the governor presents herself as an ordinary person, just like the viewer. Bandwagon: “Nine out of ten voters” and “Don’t be left out” urge you to join the crowd. A testimonial would need a different famous person praising the governor.

screens.title: Fact or Opinion?
screens.html:
A fact can be checked and proven true or false with evidence such as records, measurements, or documents. An opinion is a belief or judgment that people can reasonably disagree about.

Opinion signal words: should, best, worst, unfair, wise, wonderful, disgraceful, too much, I believe.

A number does not make a sentence a fact. “The $42,000 cost is far too high” contains a number, but “far too high” is a judgment.

example.prompt: “The city council voted 5 to 2 to raise bus fares to $2.00. The increase is unfair to working families.”
steps: Sentence 1 can be checked in council records: fact.
Sentence 2 uses “unfair,” a judgment: opinion.
example.answer: Sentence 1 is a fact; sentence 2 is an opinion.

options: The new library is the most beautiful building in the county.
The new library cost $6.5 million to build.
The library opened on September 12, 2023.
Spending $6.5 million on a library was a waste of taxpayer money.
The library holds about 80,000 books.
why: The cost can be checked in county budget records, so it is a fact statement.
The opening date can be checked, so it is a fact.
The number of books can be counted, so it is a fact statement.
check.hint: Look for judgment words. Then ask: could this be checked in a record?
check.explain: “Most beautiful” and “a waste of taxpayer money” are judgments that people can reasonably disagree about, so those two are opinions. The cost, the opening date, and the number of books can all be checked. Notice that the waste statement contains a dollar figure but is still an opinion.

screens.title: Point of View
screens.html:
Point of view is the position from which a person sees and describes events. Where someone stands (owner or worker, soldier or general, landowner or tenant) shapes which facts they notice, which facts they leave out, and the words they choose.

Two accounts of the same event can be honest and still sound completely different. Both can be primary sources. When the GED asks why two accounts differ, the answer is usually the writers’ positions and purposes, not that one of them is a liar.

Compare these two sentences about the same storm cleanup: a city official writes, “Crews cleared 90 percent of streets within three days.” A resident writes, “Our street waited a week while downtown was cleared first.” Both may be true.

check.prompt: A railroad company president and a farmer who ships grain on that railroad both write about a new law that limits freight prices. The president calls the law “a threat to progress.” The farmer calls it “long overdue relief.” Which statement best explains the difference?
options: Each writer’s economic interest shapes how he judges the law.
One of the two writers must be describing a different law.
The farmer is giving facts, while the president is giving opinions.
The president is a primary source, but the farmer is a secondary one.
why: Nothing suggests two different laws. Both writers are reacting to the same freight-price law, from opposite positions.
Both statements are opinions. “Long overdue relief” is as much a judgment as “a threat to progress.”
Both writers are participants affected by the law, writing at the time, so both are primary sources.
check.hint: What does each writer gain or lose from the law?
check.explain: The railroad loses money if freight prices are limited, and the farmer saves money, so each judges the law from his own economic position. That is point of view. Both descriptions are opinions, and both writers are primary sources.

screens.title: Cause and Effect Chains
screens.html:
A cause is why something happens. An effect is what happens as a result. Signal words: because, led to, as a result, therefore, consequently, due to.

History often works in chains: an effect becomes the cause of the next event. A cause must always come before its effect.

Example: the Dust Bowl. During World War I, high wheat prices led farmers on the southern Great Plains to plow up native grasses whose deep roots held the soil. When a long drought began in the early 1930s, crops died and the bare, dry soil was exposed. Strong winds blew it away in huge dust storms, and thousands of families left the Plains.

example.prompt: Write the Dust Bowl chain as a sequence of arrows.
steps: Start with the earliest event: high wheat prices.
Follow each “led to”: grasses plowed up → drought leaves soil bare and dry → dust storms → families leave.
example.answer: High wheat prices → grasses plowed up → drought dries bare soil → dust storms → families leave the Plains

check.prompt: Put these events in cause-and-effect order, from first cause to final effect.
choices: Families who lost their crops leave the Plains
Farmers plow up the native grasses
Strong winds blow the dry soil away in dust storms
A long drought leaves the bare soil dry
check.why: The most common mistake is putting the drought first. The drought did its damage because the grasses that held the soil had already been plowed up.
check.hint: Which event removed the protection for the soil? Start there.
check.explain: Order: (1) farmers plow up the native grasses, (2) a long drought leaves the bare soil dry, (3) winds blow the soil away in dust storms, (4) families leave the Plains. Each event made the next one possible.

screens.title: After Is Not Because: Correlation
screens.html:
Two things that change at the same time or one after the other show a correlation. A correlation alone does not prove that one thing caused the other. Something else may cause both, or the timing may be a coincidence.

To test a cause-and-effect claim, look for evidence that rules out other explanations:

  • Did the change begin after the supposed cause, or was it already happening?
  • Did similar places without the cause see the same change?
  • Is there a direct link (for example, how many people a program actually served)?

example.prompt: A large factory opened in Grant County in 2014. Does the graph prove that the factory cut unemployment in half?
steps: The rate did fall by half, from 8% to 4%.
But it was already falling before 2014, and the graph gives no information about why it fell.
example.answer: No. The graph shows a correlation in time, not proof of cause.

check.prompt: Which information would best help determine whether the factory caused Grant County’s unemployment rate to fall?
options: Unemployment rates from 2012 to 2018 in similar nearby counties that did not open a factory
The total number of products the factory made each year from 2014 to 2018
Grant County’s unemployment rate for each month of 2018, not just the yearly rate
A statement from the factory owner saying the factory helped the local economy
why: Production totals show how busy the factory was, not whether it hired the county’s unemployed workers or explains the drop.
More detail about 2018 alone shows nothing about what caused the drop that began years earlier.
The owner has a reason to give the factory credit. A claim from an interested party is not evidence of cause.
check.hint: How could you rule out other explanations that affected the whole region?
check.explain: If similar counties without a new factory saw the same drop, something else (such as a national recovery) probably explains it. If they did not, the factory becomes a stronger explanation. That comparison tests the claim. The owner’s statement is tempting, but he gains if people credit the factory.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Every stimulus: Who made it? When? Why? What does it actually show?
  • Maps: title, north, key, scale. “Where is A from B?” = start at B. Distance = squares moved × scale.
  • Data: read title, labels, units first. Bar = compare groups; line = change over time; circle = parts of a whole; table = exact values. Subtract for percentage points. Count = percent × total.
  • Supported conclusions: provable from the data. Cross out causes, predictions, and “all/every/always.”
  • Sources: primary = there, at the time; secondary = later interpretation. Ask what each can prove.
  • Bias and propaganda: loaded words, missing facts, a creator who gains. Bandwagon, name-calling, glittering generalities, testimonial, transfer, card stacking, plain folks, fear.
  • Fact = checkable; opinion = judgment. Point of view shapes what a writer includes.
  • Cause and effect: causes come first; after ≠ because of; correlation is not proof.

stimuli.html:
Description of the cartoon: A snake is drawn cut into eight separate pieces lying in a line. At the time, Britain and France were competing for control of North America, and fighting had begun on the frontier in what became the French and Indian War. A popular belief of the time held that a snake cut into pieces could come back to life if the pieces were joined before sunset.

He has white hair and a white beard and wears a tall hat decorated with white stars on a blue band. He stares directly at the viewer, frowning slightly, and points his finger straight out of the poster. Large letters read “I WANT YOU FOR U.S. ARMY.” Smaller letters underneath say “NEAREST RECRUITING STATION.”

Background: The artist James Montgomery Flagg created the poster. The United States entered World War I in April 1917, and more than four million copies of the poster were printed in 1917 and 1918.

stimuli.title: Two Sources on the Banking Crisis of 1933
stimuli.html:
Source A

Values have shrunken to fantastic levels; taxes have risen; our ability to pay has fallen; government of all kinds is faced by serious curtailment of income; the means of exchange are frozen in the currents of trade; the withered leaves of industrial enterprise lie on every side; farmers find no markets for their produce; the savings of many years in thousands of families are gone. More important, a host of unemployed citizens face the grim problem of existence, and an equally great number toil with little return. …

Finally, in our progress toward a resumption of work we require two safeguards against a return of the evils of the old order; there must be a strict supervision of all banking and credits and investments; there must be an end to speculation with other people’s money, and there must be provision for an adequate but sound currency.

—President Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1933

Source B

When Franklin D. Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, the nation was in the fourth year of the Great Depression. About one in four workers was unemployed, and thousands of banks had failed since the stock market crash of October 1929. Frightened depositors were rushing to withdraw their savings, which pushed still more banks toward collapse. Two days after his inauguration, Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday that closed the nation's banks. Congress quickly passed the Emergency Banking Act, and banks that inspectors judged to be sound began to reopen within days. Historians generally credit Roosevelt's calm, confident speeches with helping to restore public trust in the banks.

—From a U.S. history textbook chapter written for this course
stimuli.source: Source A: public-domain presidential address. Source B: original text.

stimuli.title: The Dust Bowl
stimuli.html:
During World War I (1914–1918), wheat prices were high, and new gasoline-powered tractors made it possible to plow land faster than ever. Farmers on the southern Great Plains plowed up millions of acres of native grasses, whose deep roots had held the soil in place, and planted wheat.

In the early 1930s, a long drought began. Crops died, and the bare, dry soil was exposed to the strong Plains winds. Huge dust storms followed. In May 1934, one storm carried dust all the way to Washington, D.C., and out over the Atlantic Ocean. On April 14, 1935, a day remembered as “Black Sunday,” a massive storm turned the sky dark across the region.

Many farm families lost their crops and could not pay their debts. Thousands left the Plains, many heading west to California to look for work. In April 1935, Congress passed the Soil Conservation Act, which created the Soil Conservation Service to teach farmers methods, such as planting trees as windbreaks and plowing along the natural curves of the land, that would help keep soil from blowing away.

stimuli.title: Two Accounts of a Strike (fictional)
stimuli.html:

The Harmon Mill has always paid fair wages, and our workers have been loyal for twenty years. This trouble was stirred up by outside agitators who misled good people with false promises. When business slowed this spring, we made a small, necessary adjustment to wages so that the mill could stay open and keep every worker employed. The mill will reopen Monday for all loyal employees who wish to return.

Account 2: Letter from mill worker Rose Kowalski to her sister
We walked out on Tuesday, more than three hundred of us. In April the company cut our pay by one tenth, but we still work fifty-six hours a week, and rent did not go down. No one from outside told us to strike. We voted ourselves, in the church hall. Mr. Harmon says we are disloyal, but all we ask is the pay we had before.

stimuli.title: Two Sources on a Presidential Warning (1961)
stimuli.html:
Source A

“We annually spend on military security more than the net income of all United States corporations. This conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry is new in the American experience. … In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist. We must never let the weight of this combination endanger our liberties or democratic processes. … Only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry can compel the proper meshing of the huge industrial and military machinery of defense with our peaceful methods and goals, so that security and liberty may prosper together.”

—President Dwight D. Eisenhower, Farewell Address, January 17, 1961

conjunction: joining together; unwarranted: not justified; citizenry: the citizens as a group

Source B

On January 17, 1961, three days before John F. Kennedy took office, President Dwight D. Eisenhower gave a farewell address to the nation on television. Eisenhower was a former five-star Army general who had commanded the Allied invasion of Europe during World War II, so his warning carried special weight. After World War II, the United States kept a large military even in peacetime, and private companies built many of its weapons. Eisenhower warned that this partnership, which he called the “military-industrial complex,” could gain too much influence over government. Historians note that the phrase quickly entered everyday language, and it is still used in debates over defense spending.

—From a U.S. history textbook chapter written for this course
stimuli.source: Source A: public-domain presidential address. Source B: original text.

stimuli.title: The Erie Canal
stimuli.html:
In the early 1800s, moving goods over land was slow and expensive. Shipping a ton of grain from Buffalo, on Lake Erie, to New York City cost about $100. In 1817, New York State began building a canal to connect Lake Erie with the Hudson River at Albany. When the Erie Canal was completed in 1825, it stretched 363 miles.

Because canal boats could carry heavy loads cheaply, the cost of shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City fell to less than $10. Farmers in western New York and the Great Lakes region could now sell their wheat and flour in eastern markets at a profit, so they planted more land. Their crops flowed east through the canal and down the Hudson River to New York City, which became the nation’s busiest port.

Towns along the canal grew quickly. Rochester, a village of about 1,500 people in 1820, had more than 36,000 residents by 1850. The canal’s success led other states to build canals of their own and, later, to invest in railroads to compete for western trade.

The Clearwater Dam will bring electric light to 12,000 homes that now burn kerosene. The reservoir will cover about 6,000 acres, most of it poor bottomland that floods nearly every spring. Landowners will be paid fair market value. A small number of families will need to relocate, a modest price for progress that will benefit the entire region.

Account 2: Letter from farmer Ada Lindqvist to the editor of the Clearwater Weekly
My husband’s family has farmed this valley for three generations. The company calls our land “poor bottomland,” but it is the richest soil in the county; the spring floods are what make it rich. Forty-one families will lose their homes, along with the church and the cemetery where our parents are buried. The company has offered us $18 an acre. No one asked us whether we wanted electric lights at this price.
