items.prompt: In which direction is the town of Ridgeway from the town of Carver?
options: Northeast
Southwest
Northwest
Southeast
why: You described the trip in reverse, from Ridgeway to Carver. The question says “from Carver,” so start at Carver (E2) and travel to Ridgeway (C4).
The rows are right (moving up from E to C is north), but column 2 to column 4 moves right, which is east, not west.
The columns are right (2 to 4 is east), but row E to row C moves up the map, which is north, not south.
items.hint: Start at Carver (E2). Which way do you travel to reach Ridgeway (C4)? Check rows first, then columns.
items.explain:
Step 1: Carver is in square E2 and Ridgeway is in square C4.
Step 2: Rows: going from row E to row C means moving up the map, which is north.
Step 3: Columns: going from column 2 to column 4 means moving right, which is east.
Step 4: North + east = northeast.

“Southwest” is the direction of Carver from Ridgeway, the reverse of what the question asks.

items.prompt: Using the map, about how many miles is it from Millford to Eastport, measured in a straight line from the center of one square to the center of the other?

mistakes.why: You counted the squares B2, B3, B4, and B5 as 4 squares. Center to center, count the squares you move: column 2 to column 5 is 3 squares.
You counted the squares correctly but forgot the scale. Each square is 5 miles: 3 × 5.

items.hint: Both towns are in row B. Count how many squares apart they are, then use the scale.
items.explain:
Step 1: Millford is in B2 and Eastport is in B5, both in row B.
Step 2: From column 2 to column 5 is 5 − 2 = 3 squares.
Step 3: Each square is 5 miles: 3 × 5 = 15 miles.

A common error is counting the squares B2, B3, B4, and B5 as 4 squares (20 miles). Center to center, the distance is the number of squares you move, which is 3.

items.prompt: Drag each source into the correct category.
choices: A letter a Union soldier wrote to his family in 1863
A high school textbook chapter on the Civil War published in 2019
A photograph taken at a civil rights march in 1963
A documentary film about the Great Depression made in 2010, featuring interviews with historians
The text of the Nineteenth Amendment as ratified in 1920
An encyclopedia article summarizing the causes of World War I
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the 2010 documentary under primary because it may show old film clips. As a whole, it was made decades later and presents historians’ interpretations, so it is secondary.
items.hint: Ask: Was this made by someone who was there, at the time? Or was it made later to explain the past?
items.explain:
Primary sources were created at the time by participants or witnesses: the soldier’s 1863 letter, the 1963 photograph taken at the march, and the Nineteenth Amendment itself (an original government document from 1920).

Secondary sources were created later to explain or interpret the past: the 2019 textbook, the 2010 documentary, and the encyclopedia article.

The documentary is a common trap. Even if it shows old film clips, the documentary as a whole was made decades later and presents historians’ interpretations, so it is secondary.

items.prompt: Which method of getting to work showed the largest increase in percent of workers from 2005 to 2025?
options: Worked from home
Public transit
Drove alone
Walked or biked
why: Public transit did rise, but only from 11 to 13, which is 2 percentage points. Worked from home rose 11 points.
Drove alone had the biggest change (10 points), but it was a decrease, from 68 to 58. The question asks for an increase.
Walked or biked rose from 5 to 6, only 1 percentage point. Compare the change for every method.
items.hint: For each method, subtract the 2005 value from the 2025 value.
items.explain:
Change from 2005 to 2025 for each method:
Drove alone: 58 − 68 = −10
Carpooled: 8 − 12 = −4
Public transit: 13 − 11 = +2
Walked or biked: 6 − 5 = +1
Worked from home: 15 − 4 = +11

Worked from home increased the most. “Drove alone” had the largest change, but it was a decrease, not an increase. Public transit rose, but by only 2 percentage points.

items.prompt: Add together the percent of workers who drove alone and the percent who carpooled. By how many percentage points did this combined share fall from 2005 to 2025?

mistakes.why: You found the change for driving alone only (68 − 58). Add carpooling first: 68 + 12 = 80 in 2005, and 58 + 8 = 66 in 2025.
You found the change for carpooling only (12 − 8). The question asks about the two methods combined.
That is the combined share in 2025 only. Subtract it from the 2005 combined share: 80 − 66.

items.hint: Find the combined share for each year first, then subtract.
items.explain:
2005: 68 + 12 = 80%.
2025: 58 + 8 = 66%.
Change: 80 − 66 = 14 percentage points.

You get the same answer by adding the two separate drops: 10 + 4 = 14. Answering 10 counts only the drivers who drove alone.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: A smaller share of workers drove alone in 2025 than in 2005, but it was still the most common method.
The number of workers who used public transit doubled between 2005 and 2025 as the city grew.
Fewer people worked in Carver City in 2025 than in 2005, so fewer people needed to commute.
The light-rail line that opened in 2015 caused many more workers to start working from home.
why: Transit rose from 11% to 13%, which is not a doubling, and percents do not tell you the number of riders. The graph gives no totals.
The graph shows only percents, which always add to 100. It gives no total number of workers, so it cannot show whether the workforce shrank.
The graph shows what changed, not why. Nothing on it connects the rail line to working from home.
items.hint: The graph shows percents, not numbers of people, and it does not explain why anything changed.
items.explain:
Driving alone fell from 68% to 58%, so a smaller share drove alone. In 2025, 58% is still higher than every other method (8%, 13%, 6%, 15%), so it remained the most common. Both parts of the statement are shown on the graph.

The transit choice is wrong for two reasons: 11% to 13% is not a doubling, and percents do not tell you the number of riders. The graph gives no total number of workers, so it cannot show whether fewer people worked in the city. Nothing on the graph shows that the rail line caused any change; the graph shows only what changed, not why.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from a draft of a local news article. A news article should report facts. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: The Ridgeway Public Library will extend its weekday hours beginning March 1.
Under the new schedule, the library will close at 9 p.m. instead of 6 p.m. Monday through Thursday.
The change will cost about $42,000 per year, according to the county budget office.
The county board approved the plan by a vote of 4 to 1 on Tuesday.
Keeping the doors open later is the smartest investment the county has made in years.
Library staff said the new hours will be covered by hiring two part-time workers.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about the $42,000 cost. It contains a number, but it reports a figure from the budget office that can be checked. The opinion is the sentence calling the change “the smartest investment.”
items.hint: Look for a sentence with a judgment word that people could reasonably disagree about.
items.explain:
“Keeping the doors open later is the smartest investment the county has made in years” is an opinion. “Smartest investment” is a judgment, and there is no way to prove it true or false.

Every other sentence can be checked: the start date, the new closing time, the cost reported by the budget office, the 4-to-1 vote, and what the staff said. The sentence about cost contains a number, but numbers do not make a sentence a fact or an opinion; what matters is whether it can be verified.

items.prompt: What was Benjamin Franklin’s main message in the 1754 cartoon?
options: The colonies needed to unite in order to survive the threat they faced.
The colonies should break away and declare independence from Great Britain.
New England was stronger than the other colonies and should lead them.
Snakes were a serious and growing danger to settlers on the frontier.
why: This uses later history. The cartoon was reused during the Revolution, but in 1754 the colonies were fighting alongside Britain against France, and nothing in it calls for breaking away.
New England is just one of the eight pieces. The cartoon does not rank the colonies or name a leader.
This reads the symbol literally. The cut snake stands for the divided colonies, as the caption “JOIN, or DIE” shows.
items.hint: Think about the popular belief described in the background, and the words printed under the snake.
items.explain:
The snake is cut into separate pieces, one for each colony or region. The caption says “JOIN, or DIE,” and the background explains the belief that a cut snake could live again only if its pieces were joined. Franklin’s message: the colonies must unite or be defeated one by one during the conflict with France.

The independence choice is a common mistake. The cartoon was later reused during the American Revolution, but in 1754 the colonies were fighting alongside Britain against France, and nothing in the cartoon calls for breaking away from Britain. New England is just one segment; the cartoon does not rank the colonies. The snake is a symbol, not a warning about real snakes.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the poster.

The poster uses Uncle Sam, a well-known symbol of the United States, so that viewers connect the feelings they have about their country with joining the army. This propaganda technique is called {{0}}. The main purpose of the poster was to {{1}}. Because it was created to persuade, the poster is most useful to a historian as evidence of {{2}}.

options: transfer
bandwagon
testimonial
card stacking
why: Bandwagon would say that everyone else is joining. The poster speaks to “YOU” alone and says nothing about other people.
Testimonial uses a real famous person’s endorsement. Uncle Sam is a symbol of the nation, not a celebrity.
Card stacking presents a one-sided list of facts. The poster gives no facts at all.

options: persuade men to enlist in the U.S. Army
report how many soldiers were already serving
explain why the United States entered the war
ask citizens to grow more food
why: The poster gives no numbers of any kind.
The poster gives no reasons for the war; it simply calls on the viewer to join.
Nothing on the poster mentions food. It names the army and a recruiting station.

options: how the government tried to build public support for the war
the exact number of men who enlisted because of the poster
how every American felt about the war in 1917
the battles the U.S. Army fought in Europe
why: A poster cannot show how many people responded to it. That would require enlistment records.
A persuasive poster shows what its makers wanted people to feel, not how the public actually felt.
The poster was made to recruit soldiers; it says nothing about battles.

items.hint: Which technique links an idea to a respected symbol? Then read the words printed on the poster.
items.explain:
Blank 1: transfer. Transfer links a cause to a respected symbol (here, Uncle Sam) so the viewer’s feelings for the symbol carry over to the cause. Bandwagon would say “everyone is joining”; testimonial would use a real famous person’s endorsement; card stacking would present a one-sided list of facts. None of these appear in the description.

Blank 2: persuade men to enlist. The words “I WANT YOU FOR U.S. ARMY” and “NEAREST RECRUITING STATION” tell viewers to sign up. The poster gives no numbers and no reasons for the war, and it says nothing about food.

Blank 3: how the government tried to build support. A persuasive poster shows what its makers wanted people to think and do. It cannot show how many men actually enlisted because of it or how all Americans felt.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why Source A is a primary source and Source B is a secondary source?
options: Source A was created by a participant during the events; Source B was written later to explain them.
Source A is more accurate than Source B because it comes directly from the president himself.
Source A expresses the speaker’s opinions, while Source B contains only facts about the crisis.
Source A is about the whole national economy, while Source B is only about the nation’s banks.
why: Source type is about who made the source and when, not accuracy. A speech is meant to persuade and shows one person’s view.
Source B is not purely factual: its last sentence reports an interpretation (“Historians generally credit…”). And opinions do not decide source type.
The topic of a source does not make it primary or secondary. Both sources discuss banks and the wider economy.
items.hint: The difference between primary and secondary sources is about who created the source and when, not about accuracy.
items.explain:
Source A is President Roosevelt’s own speech, given on March 4, 1933, as the crisis was happening, so it is a primary source. Source B is a textbook passage written long afterward that explains the events and includes historians’ judgments, so it is a secondary source.

Primary sources are not automatically more accurate; a speech is meant to persuade and shows one person’s view. Source B is not purely factual either: its last sentence reports an interpretation (“Historians generally credit…”). Topic does not determine source type.

items.prompt: Which pieces of information appear in Source B but not in Source A? Select two answers.
options: About how large a share of workers was unemployed
That Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday that closed the nation’s banks
That many families had lost their savings
That farmers could not find markets for their crops
That Roosevelt called for strict supervision of banking, credit, and investments
why: Source A says this directly: “the savings of many years in thousands of families are gone.”
Source A says this directly: “farmers find no markets for their produce.”
Source A says this directly: “there must be a strict supervision of all banking and credits and investments.”
items.hint: For each choice, check Source A first. If you can find it there, it is not a correct answer.
items.explain:
Correct: Source B says “About one in four workers was unemployed.” Source A mentions “a host of unemployed citizens” but never gives a share or number. Source B also describes the national bank holiday, which happened two days after the speech, so Source A could not include it.

Incorrect: Lost savings (“the savings of many years in thousands of families are gone”), farmers without markets (“farmers find no markets for their produce”), and the call for supervision of banking (“there must be a strict supervision of all banking and credits and investments”) all appear in Source A.

items.prompt: Which sequence of events correctly shows the chain of causes and effects described in the passage?
options: High wheat prices → native grasses plowed up → drought leaves soil bare and dry → wind carries soil away in dust storms
Dust storms → native grasses plowed up → high wheat prices → drought begins on the southern Plains
Soil Conservation Service created → drought begins → farmers plow native grasses → dust storms
Families move to California → farms are abandoned → wheat prices rise → dust storms sweep the Plains
why: This reverses the chain. The dust storms were the final effect; they came after the plowing and the drought, not before.
The Soil Conservation Service was created in 1935 as a response to the dust storms, so it cannot be the first cause.
Families moved to California as an effect of the disaster. The passage says they left after losing their crops.
items.hint: Find the earliest event in the passage and follow the words that show what each event led to.
items.explain:
Step 1: High wheat prices during World War I encouraged farmers to plow up native grasses.
Step 2: The grasses’ deep roots had held the soil; without them, the soil was unprotected.
Step 3: The drought of the early 1930s killed crops and left the bare soil dry.
Step 4: Strong winds carried the soil away in dust storms.

The other sequences put effects before causes. The Soil Conservation Service was created in 1935 as a response to the dust storms, and families moved to California as an effect of the disaster, not as a cause of it.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the two accounts describe the strike so differently?
options: Each writer’s position in the conflict shapes which facts are included and how the strike is described.
Account 1 is a primary source, while Account 2 is a secondary source written many years after the strike.
The two writers are describing two different strikes that happened at the Harmon Mill in the same year.
Account 2 was written to be printed in a newspaper, while Account 1 was a private note never meant for others.
why: Both accounts were written at the time by people involved in the strike, so both are primary sources. Rose Kowalski’s letter is not a later history.
Both accounts describe the same 1911 strike at the Harmon Mill; the introduction says so.
This reverses the facts. Account 2 is a private letter to a sister, and Account 1 was printed in the company newsletter.
items.hint: Who wrote each account, and what does each writer want the reader to believe?
items.explain:
Both accounts describe the same 1911 strike, and both are primary sources written at the time. They differ because of point of view. The owner calls the pay cut a “small, necessary adjustment,” blames “outside agitators” (name-calling), and calls returning workers “loyal.” The worker gives specific details the owner leaves out (a one-tenth pay cut, fifty-six-hour weeks, rent that did not go down) and says the workers voted to strike themselves.

Account 2 is a private letter to a sister, and Account 1 was printed in the company newsletter, so the newspaper choice reverses the facts. Account 2 is not a later secondary source; it was written by a participant during the strike.

items.prompt: According to the circle graph, how many million dollars more does Ashton County plan to spend on public safety than on parks and recreation?

mistakes.why: That is the difference in percentage points (35 − 10). Turn it into dollars: 25% of $60 million = 0.25 × 60.
That is the full public safety amount (35% of $60 million = $21 million). Subtract the parks amount, $6 million.
That is the parks amount only (10% of $60 million). The question asks how much more goes to public safety.

items.hint: Find each slice in dollars (percent × $60 million), then subtract.
items.explain:
Public safety: 35% of $60 million = 0.35 × 60 = $21 million.
Parks and recreation: 10% of $60 million = 0.10 × 60 = $6 million.
Difference: 21 − 6 = $15 million.

Shortcut: (35 − 10)% = 25%, and 0.25 × 60 = 15. Answering 25 stops at the percentage points and never converts to dollars.

items.prompt: The police chief says, “Doubling our downtown foot patrols in 2021 caused the drop in burglaries.” Which additional information would best help a reader evaluate this claim?
options: Burglary counts for the same years in similar cities that did not add foot patrols
The number of officers who volunteered for downtown foot patrol duty in 2021
A survey of downtown shop owners asking whether they like the new foot patrols
Oakton’s burglary counts for 2025 and 2026, after the years shown on the graph
why: Knowing how many officers volunteered shows how the patrols were staffed, not whether they caused the drop in burglaries.
Whether shop owners like the patrols is an opinion survey. It does not show what caused burglaries to fall.
More years of Oakton data would show whether the low numbers lasted, but not whether something other than the patrols caused them.
items.hint: How could you rule out other explanations that affected many cities at once?
items.explain:
The graph shows burglaries fell from 380 in 2020 to 300 in 2021 and kept falling. But burglaries were already falling before 2021 (410, 395, 380), and something affecting the whole region could explain the drop. Comparing similar cities that did not add patrols tests the claim: if their burglaries fell just as much, the patrols probably were not the cause.

The shop owner survey is tempting, but liking the patrols is an opinion and does not show cause.

items.prompt: In which direction is the town of Cedar Gap from the town of Brandon?
options: Northwest
Southeast
Northeast
Southwest
why: You described the trip in reverse, from Cedar Gap to Brandon. The question says “from Brandon,” so start at Brandon (D4).
The rows are right (D to B moves up the map, north), but column 4 to column 2 moves left, which is west, not east.
The columns are right (4 to 2 is west), but row D to row B moves up the map, which is north, not south.
items.hint: Start at Brandon (D4) and travel to Cedar Gap (B2). Rows first, then columns.
items.explain:
Step 1: Brandon is in D4 and Cedar Gap is in B2.
Step 2: Rows: D to B moves up the map: north.
Step 3: Columns: 4 to 2 moves left: west.
Step 4: North + west = northwest.

“Southeast” is the direction of Brandon from Cedar Gap, the reverse of the question.

items.prompt: Using the map, how many miles is it from Westover to Elmira, measured in a straight line from the center of one square to the center of the other?

mistakes.why: You counted all five squares, C1 through C5. Center to center, count the squares you move: column 1 to column 5 is 4 squares.
You counted the squares correctly but forgot the scale. Each square is 10 miles: 4 × 10.

items.hint: Both towns are in row C. Count the squares you move, then use the scale.
items.explain:
Step 1: Westover is in C1 and Elmira is in C5, both in row C.
Step 2: From column 1 to column 5 is 5 − 1 = 4 squares.
Step 3: Each square is 10 miles: 4 × 10 = 40 miles.

Counting all five squares gives 50 miles, but you do not move through the square you start in.

items.prompt: Drag each source into the correct category.
choices: A radio speech President Franklin D. Roosevelt gave to the nation in 1933
A museum website article from 2018 explaining the causes of the Great Depression
A ration book issued to an American family in 1943, during World War II
A college textbook chapter on World War II published in 2015
A photograph taken at the first Earth Day rally in 1970
A biography of Harriet Tubman written in 2004
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the ration book under secondary because it is not a written account. Objects and official records made at the time, like a ration book, are primary sources.
items.hint: Ask: Was this made at the time, by someone involved? Objects and records count too.
items.explain:
Primary sources were made at the time by participants or witnesses: Roosevelt’s 1933 radio speech, the 1943 ration book (an official record that a family actually used), and the 1970 photograph taken at the rally.

Secondary sources were made later to explain the past: the 2018 museum article, the 2015 textbook, and the 2004 biography.

items.prompt: Which heating fuel showed the largest decrease in percent of households from 2000 to 2024?
options: Heating oil
Natural gas
Electricity
Wood
why: Natural gas fell from 55 to 48, a drop of 7 percentage points. Heating oil fell 9 points. The tallest bars do not always show the biggest change.
Electricity had the largest change (13 points), but it rose from 25 to 38. The question asks for a decrease.
Wood fell from 4 to 2, only 2 percentage points. Compare the change for every fuel.
items.hint: For each fuel, subtract the 2000 value from the 2024 value. Look for the most negative result.
items.explain:
Change from 2000 to 2024 for each fuel:
Natural gas: 48 − 55 = −7
Electricity: 38 − 25 = +13
Heating oil: 6 − 15 = −9
Wood: 2 − 4 = −2
Solar and other: 6 − 1 = +5

Heating oil decreased the most. Electricity changed the most, but it was an increase.

items.prompt: Add together the percent of households that heated with heating oil and the percent that heated with wood. By how many percentage points did this combined share fall from 2000 to 2024?

mistakes.why: You found the change for heating oil only (15 − 6). Add wood first: 15 + 4 = 19 in 2000, and 6 + 2 = 8 in 2024.
You found the change for wood only (4 − 2). The question asks about the two fuels combined.
That is the combined share in 2024 only. Subtract it from the 2000 combined share: 19 − 8.

items.hint: Find the combined share for each year first, then subtract.
items.explain:
2000: 15 + 4 = 19%.
2024: 6 + 2 = 8%.
Change: 19 − 8 = 11 percentage points.

You get the same answer by adding the two separate drops: 9 + 2 = 11. Answering 9 counts heating oil only.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: Natural gas was still the most common heating fuel in 2024, though its share was smaller than in 2000.
The number of Linwood homes heated with electricity more than doubled between 2000 and 2024.
The heat pump rebates that began in 2010 caused households to switch from heating oil to electricity.
Fewer households existed in Linwood in 2024 than in 2000, so total demand for home heat went down.
why: The graph shows percents, not numbers of homes, and 25% to 38% is not even a doubling of the share.
The graph shows what changed, not why. It does not connect the rebates to any household’s choice of fuel.
The graph gives no total number of households. Percents always add to 100, whatever the size of the town.
items.hint: The graph shows percents, not numbers of homes, and it does not explain why anything changed.
items.explain:
Natural gas fell from 55% to 48%, so its share was smaller. In 2024, 48% is still higher than every other fuel (38%, 6%, 2%, 6%), so it remained the most common. Both parts are shown on the graph.

The electricity choice treats a percent as a count; the rebate choice claims a cause the graph cannot show; and the graph has no totals, so it cannot show how many households existed.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from a draft of a local news article. A news article should report facts. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: The Elmira City Council voted 6 to 1 on Monday to build a skate park in Riverside Park.
The skate park will cost $380,000, according to the city parks department.
A state grant will pay $150,000 of the cost, and the city will pay the rest.
This skate park is exactly what our bored, restless teenagers have needed for years.
Construction is scheduled to begin in April and end by August.
The parks director said the park will be open from 8 a.m. to dusk every day.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about the $150,000 state grant. It contains numbers, but the grant amount can be checked in city records. The opinion is the claim about what teenagers have needed.
items.hint: Find the sentence with judgment words that cannot be checked in a record.
items.explain:
“This skate park is exactly what our bored, restless teenagers have needed for years” is an opinion. “Exactly what they have needed” is a judgment, and “bored, restless” are loaded words. People could reasonably disagree.

Every other sentence can be checked: the vote, the cost, the grant, the schedule, and what the parks director said.

items.prompt: What is the main message of the cartoon?
options: Many citizens will put more effort into buying a product than into voting in local elections.
Cities should move their polling places into busy stores to make voting much more convenient.
New phones have become too expensive for most families in the city to afford to buy.
Long lines at polling places on Election Day are keeping many citizens from casting a vote.
why: This takes the drawing too literally. The cartoonist is criticizing what citizens choose to wait for, not proposing a new place to vote.
Nothing in the cartoon mentions price. The crowd outside the store shows that people are eager to buy, not that they cannot afford it.
This reverses the cartoon. The polling place has no line at all; the long line is outside the store.
items.hint: Compare the two lines. What is the cartoonist criticizing about what people are willing to wait for?
items.explain:
The cartoon contrasts an empty polling place with a huge line for a new phone. The man’s question, “Who has time to wait in line for that?”, is ironic: he is already waiting in a very long line. The message is that many citizens care more about a new product than about voting in local elections.

The long-lines choice is tempting if you skim, but the line in the cartoon is at the store, not the polling place.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the poster.

The poster shows people from many walks of life all holding bonds and says “EVERYBODY’S BUYING!” This propaganda technique is called {{0}}. The main purpose of the poster was to {{1}}. Because it was created to persuade, the poster is most useful to a historian as evidence of {{2}}.

options: bandwagon
transfer
testimonial
fear
why: Transfer links a cause to a respected symbol such as the flag or Uncle Sam. No such symbol appears on this poster.
Testimonial uses a famous person’s endorsement. The people shown are ordinary, unnamed citizens.
Fear warns of danger. The poster shows smiling people and makes no threat.

options: persuade civilians to buy war bonds
report how many families owned war bonds
recruit young men into the armed forces
explain how war bonds earn interest
why: The “9 out of 10” claim is there to pressure the viewer, not to report a verified count.
The poster asks viewers to buy bonds, not to enlist. It shows a grandmother and a schoolteacher, not recruits.
Interest is mentioned only in the background note, not on the poster, which simply urges people to buy.

options: how the government encouraged civilians to help pay for the war
the actual share of families that owned war bonds
how every American felt about the war in the 1940s
the battles that war bonds helped to pay for
why: A persuasive poster cannot be trusted as a count. The “9 out of 10” figure was chosen to pressure viewers; bond sales records would show the real share.
A poster shows what its makers wanted people to feel, not what the public actually felt.
The poster does not mention any battles.

items.hint: What are all the people on the poster doing, and what does the poster want you to do?
items.explain:
Blank 1: bandwagon. “EVERYBODY’S BUYING!” and “DON’T BE THE ONE” urge the viewer to join the crowd. There is no symbol (transfer), no famous person (testimonial), and no threat (fear).

Blank 2: persuade civilians to buy war bonds. The poster ends with “BUY BONDS TODAY.”

Blank 3: how the government encouraged civilians to help pay for the war. The poster shows the message its makers wanted to spread. Its “9 out of 10” claim is part of the persuasion, so it is not reliable evidence of how many families actually owned bonds.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why Source A is a primary source and Source B is a secondary source?
options: Source A is Eisenhower’s own words from 1961; Source B was written later to explain and interpret them.
Source A is more trustworthy than Source B because a president knows more than any historian could.
Source A gives the speaker’s opinions, while Source B reports only facts about the address.
Source A is about the armed forces, while Source B is mostly about Eisenhower’s life story.
why: Source type depends on who made the source and when, not on trustworthiness. A farewell speech also reflects one person’s view and purpose.
Source B also contains interpretation: “his warning carried special weight” is a judgment. And opinions do not decide source type.
Both sources are about the same warning. Topic does not make a source primary or secondary.
items.hint: Primary or secondary depends on who created the source and when.
items.explain:
Source A is President Eisenhower’s own speech, given on January 17, 1961, so it is a primary source. Source B is a textbook passage written later that explains the speech and reports how historians view it, so it is a secondary source.

Primary does not mean more trustworthy, and Source B is not purely factual: “his warning carried special weight” is the author’s judgment.

items.prompt: Which pieces of information appear in Source B but not in Source A? Select two answers.
options: That Eisenhower had commanded the Allied invasion of Europe in World War II
That the speech was given three days before John F. Kennedy took office
That the partnership of the military and the arms industry was new in America
That citizens must guard against unwarranted influence by the military-industrial complex
That only alert and informed citizens can keep security and liberty in balance
why: Source A says this directly: “This conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry is new in the American experience.”
Source A says this directly: “we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence… by the military-industrial complex.”
Source A says this directly: “Only an alert and knowledgeable citizenry can compel the proper meshing…”
items.hint: For each choice, look for it in Source A first. If it is there, it is not a correct answer.
items.explain:
Correct: Only Source B describes Eisenhower’s background as the commander of the Allied invasion of Europe, and only Source B places the speech three days before Kennedy took office. Source A is the speech itself and mentions neither.

Incorrect: The newness of the military-arms partnership, the warning against unwarranted influence, and the call for an alert citizenry all come straight from Source A.

items.prompt: Which sequence of events correctly shows the chain of causes and effects described in the passage?
options: Canal completed → shipping costs fall → western farmers sell more crops in the East → New York City becomes the busiest port
New York City becomes the busiest port → canal completed → shipping costs fall → western farmers plant more land
Other states build railroads → shipping costs fall → canal completed → Rochester grows into a city
Farmers plant more land → canal completed → shipping costs fall → New York State begins building a canal
why: This puts an effect first. New York City became the busiest port because crops flowed through the canal, so the port’s growth came after the canal.
Other states built canals and railroads after the Erie Canal succeeded. Their projects were an effect, not a cause.
New York began building in 1817, before the canal was completed in 1825, and farmers planted more land only after shipping became cheap.
items.hint: Look for signal words such as “Because,” “so,” and “led.” A cause must come before its effect.
items.explain:
Step 1: The canal was completed in 1825.
Step 2: Shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City fell from about $100 to less than $10.
Step 3: Western farmers could sell wheat and flour in the East at a profit, so they planted more land and shipped more crops.
Step 4: Crops flowed through the canal to New York City, which became the nation’s busiest port.

The other sequences put effects before causes. The signal word “Because” at the start of the second paragraph shows that cheap shipping came from the canal.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the two accounts describe the dam project so differently?
options: Each writer’s stake in the project shapes which facts are stressed and the words used to describe the land.
Account 1 is a primary source, while Account 2 is a secondary source written long after the dam was built.
The two writers are describing two different dam projects planned for two different valleys in the state.
Account 1 contains only facts that can be checked, while Account 2 contains only the writer’s personal opinions.
why: Both accounts were written at the time by people directly involved, so both are primary sources.
Both accounts describe the same Clearwater Dam; the introduction says so, and Account 2 quotes the company’s description of the land.
Account 1 also contains opinions, such as “a modest price for progress,” and Account 2 contains checkable facts, such as the $18-an-acre offer and the 41 families.
items.hint: What does each writer stand to gain or lose if the dam is built?
items.explain:
Both accounts describe the same project, and both are primary sources. They differ because of point of view. The company engineer stresses benefits (light for 12,000 homes), calls the land “poor bottomland,” says “a small number of families,” and calls the cost “a modest price for progress.” The farmer stresses what will be lost: rich soil, 41 homes, a church, a cemetery, and an offer of only $18 an acre.

The facts-versus-opinions choice is tempting, but each account mixes checkable facts with judgments.

items.prompt: According to the circle graph, how many million dollars more does Fairmont City collect from property taxes than from state aid each year?

mistakes.why: That is the difference in percentage points (45 − 15). Turn it into dollars: 30% of $45 million = 0.30 × 45.
That is the full property tax amount (45% of $45 million). Subtract the state aid amount, $6.75 million.
That is the state aid amount only (15% of $45 million). The question asks how much more comes from property taxes.

items.hint: Find each slice in dollars (percent × $45 million), then subtract.
items.explain:
Property taxes: 45% of $45 million = 0.45 × 45 = $20.25 million.
State aid: 15% of $45 million = 0.15 × 45 = $6.75 million.
Difference: 20.25 − 6.75 = $13.5 million.

Shortcut: (45 − 15)% = 30%, and 0.30 × 45 = 13.5. Answering 30 stops at the percentage points.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph and the information above it?
options: Youth arrests fell after the program began, but the graph alone cannot show the program caused it.
The summer jobs program cut Riverton’s youth arrest rate by more than half within three years.
Youth arrests in Riverton did not begin to fall until the year the summer jobs program started.
More Riverton teenagers held summer jobs in 2022 than in 2016, so fewer of them were arrested.
why: The rate fell from 33 in 2019 to 26 in 2022, much less than half. And the graph cannot show that the program caused any of the drop.
The graph shows arrests were already falling before 2019: 42, 40, 37. The decline did not start with the program.
The graph shows arrests only. It gives no numbers of teens with jobs, and it cannot show why arrests fell.
items.hint: Check when the decline started. Then ask whether the graph shows why it happened.
items.explain:
The rate fell from 33 in 2019 to 26 in 2022, after the program began. But it was already falling before the program (42 in 2016, 40 in 2017, 37 in 2018), and the graph gives no information about why. So the supported conclusion is that arrests fell after the program began, while the graph alone cannot prove the program was the cause.

The “cut by more than half” choice is wrong twice: the numbers do not support it, and it claims a cause.

items.prompt: In which direction is the town of Kestrel from the town of Pruitt?
options: Northeast
Southwest
Northwest
Southeast
why: You described the trip in reverse, from Kestrel to Pruitt. Start at Pruitt (D2), because the question says “from Pruitt.”
Row D to row B is north, which is right, but column 2 to column 4 moves right, which is east, not west.
Column 2 to column 4 is east, which is right, but row D to row B moves up the map, which is north, not south.
items.explain: Pruitt is in D2 and Kestrel is in B4. Rows: D to B moves up the map (north). Columns: 2 to 4 moves right (east). North + east = northeast. “Southwest” is the reverse trip, from Kestrel to Pruitt.

items.prompt: A bus travels straight south from Ardmore to Pruitt. Measured from the center of one square to the center of the other, how many miles does it travel?

mistakes.why: You counted all four rows, A through D, as squares moved. From row A to row D you move 3 squares: 3 × 3 miles.
You counted the 3 squares but did not use the scale. Each square is 3 miles: 3 × 3.

items.explain: Ardmore is in A2 and Pruitt is in D2, the same column. Row A to row D is 3 squares. 3 × 3 miles = 9 miles. Counting all four rows gives 12, but you do not move through the square you start in.

items.prompt: By how many percentage points did the West’s share of the U.S. population increase from 1910 to 2020?

mistakes.why: That is the West’s share in 2020 only. Find the change: 23.7 − 7.7.
You added the two values. To find how much the share grew, subtract: 23.7 − 7.7.
That is the percent increase (16 ÷ 7.7). The question asks for percentage points, so just subtract.

items.explain:
2020: 23.7%. 1910: 7.7%.
Change: 23.7 − 7.7 = 16.0 percentage points.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is supported by the graph and the information above it?
options: The Northeast held a smaller share of the U.S. population in 2020 than it did in 1910.
Fewer people lived in the Northeast in 2020 than in 1910, because many of them moved away.
Warm weather and new jobs caused millions of Americans to move to the South and the West.
More than half of all U.S. residents lived in the South by the time of the 2020 census.
why: This treats a share as a count. The Northeast’s share fell, but the U.S. grew from about 92 million to 331 million: 28.0% of 92 million is about 26 million, and 17.4% of 331 million is about 58 million. The number of people rose.
The graph shows how the shares changed, not why. Nothing in it mentions weather or jobs.
The South had 38.1% in 2020. That is the largest share, but it is less than half (50%).
items.explain:
The Northeast’s share fell from 28.0% to 17.4%, so it held a smaller share in 2020. That is all the statement claims, and the graph shows it.

The tempting wrong answer says fewer people lived in the Northeast. But a share is not a count: about 0.280 × 92 million ≈ 26 million in 1910, and about 0.174 × 331 million ≈ 58 million in 2020. The Northeast’s population grew even as its share shrank.

items.prompt: A student is researching how the Great Depression affected ordinary families. Which are primary sources? Select two answers.
options: A 1933 letter from a farmer to the president describing how his family lost their farm
Photographs of a line of people waiting for free bread, taken in a city in 1932
A 2009 textbook chapter explaining the programs of the New Deal
A 1998 documentary in which historians discuss the causes of the Depression
An encyclopedia article summarizing the stock market crash of 1929
why: A textbook written in 2009 explains the past; it is a secondary source.
A documentary made in 1998 presents historians’ interpretations decades later; it is secondary.
An encyclopedia article summarizes events after the fact; it is secondary, even though it is about 1929.
items.explain: The farmer’s 1933 letter and the 1932 photographs were made at the time by people who lived through or witnessed the Depression, so they are primary sources. The textbook, the documentary, and the encyclopedia article were all created later to explain the period, so they are secondary.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the ad.

When Tasha Grant tells viewers to vote for Reyes, the ad uses the technique called {{0}}. When the narrator calls Shaw “a career politician who has never worked a real job,” the ad uses {{1}}. Because the ad was paid for by Reyes’s supporters, it is most useful as evidence of {{2}}.

options: testimonial
bandwagon
plain folks
card stacking
why: Bandwagon says everyone is doing it. Grant speaks only for herself, as a famous person endorsing Reyes.
Plain folks is when the candidate presents himself as an ordinary person. Here a famous athlete speaks for him.
Card stacking lists only helpful facts. Grant gives no facts; she gives her personal endorsement.

options: name-calling
glittering generalities
transfer
bandwagon
why: Glittering generalities are vague positive words. This line attacks the opponent with a negative label.
Transfer links a cause to a respected symbol. No symbol is used in this line.
Bandwagon urges you to join the crowd. This line attacks a person instead.

options: how the Reyes campaign tried to win votes
whether Shaw has ever held a job outside government
how most Bayport voters felt about the two candidates
which candidate would make better decisions for the city
why: The ad’s claim about Shaw is an insult from her opponent’s supporters, not reliable evidence. Her work history would have to be checked in other records.
An ad shows what its makers wanted voters to think, not what voters actually thought.
An ad made to win votes cannot show which candidate would govern better.

items.explain: Testimonial: a famous person (Grant) endorses the candidate. Name-calling: “career politician who has never worked a real job” is a negative label instead of a reason. Because Reyes’s supporters paid for it, the ad is good evidence of how the campaign tried to win votes, and weak evidence of facts about Shaw or of what voters believed.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from a draft of a news article. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: The Harbor History Museum reopened Saturday after an 18-month renovation.
The renovation cost $2.3 million, paid for by private donors and a state grant.
The museum added a new gallery about the city’s fishing industry.
Adult tickets now cost $12, up from $10.
Raising ticket prices was a terrible decision that will drive families away.
The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about the $12 ticket price. It reports a price increase, which can be checked. The opinion is the sentence calling the increase “a terrible decision.”
items.explain: “Raising ticket prices was a terrible decision that will drive families away” is an opinion: “terrible decision” is a judgment, and “will drive families away” is a prediction. Every other sentence (the reopening, the cost, the new gallery, the ticket prices, the hours) can be checked.

items.prompt: A study found that cities with more public libraries per person tend to have higher voter turnout. A commentator concludes, “Building more libraries will make people vote.” Which statement best evaluates this conclusion?
options: It is not proven: the pattern is a correlation, and another factor, such as education, could explain both.
It is proven, because the same pattern appeared in many different cities across the whole country.
It is false, because libraries are places for reading and have no connection to civic life at all.
It would be proven if researchers measured voter turnout in those same cities for more elections.
why: Seeing the same pattern in many places shows a strong correlation, not a cause. Something else could still drive both libraries and turnout everywhere.
The study does not show the claim is false either. It just cannot prove a cause. Calling it false goes beyond the evidence too.
More elections would show the same correlation again, but it would still not rule out a third factor.
items.explain: Libraries and turnout rise together, which is a correlation. A third factor, such as residents’ education or income, could lead to both more libraries and more voting. To test the cause, you would need evidence such as turnout before and after new libraries opened, compared with similar cities that built none. The “many cities” answer is tempting, but a pattern repeated many times is still only a pattern.

items.prompt: In which direction is the town of Sumner from the town of Briar?
options: Southwest
Northeast
Southeast
Northwest
why: You described the trip in reverse, from Sumner to Briar. Start at Briar (A3), because the question says “from Briar.”
Row A to row D is south, which is right, but column 3 to column 1 moves left, which is west, not east.
Column 3 to column 1 is west, which is right, but row A to row D moves down the map, which is south, not north.
items.explain: Briar is in A3 and Sumner is in D1. Rows: A to D moves down the map (south). Columns: 3 to 1 moves left (west). South + west = southwest. “Northeast” is the reverse trip.

items.prompt: How many miles is it from Calvert to Linden, measured in a straight line from the center of one square to the center of the other?

mistakes.why: You counted all four squares in row B. Center to center, you move from column 1 to column 4, which is 3 squares: 3 × 6.
You counted the 3 squares but did not use the scale. Each square is 6 miles: 3 × 6.

items.explain: Calvert is in B1 and Linden is in B4, the same row. Column 1 to column 4 is 3 squares. 3 × 6 miles = 18 miles.

items.prompt: By how many thousand people did Westlake County’s population grow from 1990 to 2010?

mistakes.why: You started from 1980 (180 − 120). The question starts at 1990: 180 − 135.
You used the 2020 value (171 − 135). The question ends at 2010: 180 − 135.

items.explain:
1990: 135 thousand. 2010: 180 thousand.
Growth: 180 − 135 = 45 thousand people.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is supported by the graph?
options: The population rose in each decade from 1980 to 2010 and then fell between 2010 and 2020.
A large factory closing after 2010 caused thousands of residents to leave Westlake County.
The county’s population roughly doubled between the 1980 census and the 2020 census.
The share of county residents who were age 65 or older grew between 2010 and 2020.
why: The graph shows that the population fell after 2010, but not why. Nothing in it mentions a factory.
Doubling 120 thousand would be 240 thousand. The 2020 population was 171 thousand, an increase of less than half.
The graph shows total population only. It gives no information about residents’ ages.
items.explain: 120 → 135 → 162 → 180 rises every decade, and 180 → 171 is a decline. Both parts of the statement are shown. The factory answer claims a cause the graph cannot show; the doubling answer fails the arithmetic (2 × 120 = 240, not 171); and the graph has no age data.

items.prompt: A student is researching the civil rights movement. Which are secondary sources? Select two answers.
options: A biography of civil rights leader Fannie Lou Hamer written in 2014
A 2005 documentary in which historians explain the Montgomery bus boycott
A speech delivered at the March on Washington in August 1963
The text of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 as passed by Congress
A photograph taken during the Selma to Montgomery march in 1965
why: A speech given at the march, by a participant, at the time, is a primary source.
The text of a law is an original government document from the time. It is a primary source.
A photograph taken at the march records the event as it happened. It is a primary source.
items.explain: The 2014 biography and the 2005 documentary were created decades later by people interpreting the movement, so they are secondary sources. The 1963 speech, the 1964 law, and the 1965 photograph were all made at the time by participants or witnesses, so they are primary.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the flyer.

The huge American flag above the stadium is an example of the technique called {{0}}. The flyer lists jobs and visitor spending but never mentions the $300 million in city funds, an example of {{1}}. A reader should be especially cautious about the flyer because {{2}}.

options: transfer
testimonial
bandwagon
name-calling
why: Testimonial uses a famous person’s endorsement. The flyer shows a flag, not a person.
Bandwagon says everyone is doing it. The flag image does not mention other people.
Name-calling attacks someone with a label. The flag image attacks no one.

options: card stacking
glittering generalities
plain folks
fear
why: Glittering generalities are vague feel-good words. The flyer gives specific claims; the problem is that it leaves out the cost.
Plain folks presents the speaker as an ordinary person. The flyer does not do this.
Fear warns of danger. The flyer lists only benefits.

options: the group that paid for it is funded by owners who would benefit if the measure passes
the flyer was mailed to voters instead of being shown on television
the flyer gives specific numbers, which makes it a primary source
the stadium has not been built yet, so the flyer must be a secondary source
why: How the flyer reached voters does not make it more or less trustworthy. Who paid for it does.
Numbers do not decide source type, and a primary source still needs to be checked for bias.
A flyer made at the time of the vote by people involved is a primary source, whether or not the stadium exists yet.

items.explain: Transfer: the flag links the stadium to the respect people feel for their country. Card stacking: the flyer shows only the benefits and leaves out the $300 million cost. Caution: the small print shows that the team owners, who would gain from a new stadium, funded the flyer. A creator who gains if you agree is a key clue to bias.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from a draft of a news article. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.

The market will be held every Saturday from 7 a.m. to noon.
About 40 local farms and bakeries have signed up to sell there.
Vendors will pay $25 per week for a booth.
Moving the market downtown is the best thing the city has ever done for small businesses.
Free parking will be available in the city garage on Main Street.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about the $25 booth fee. It contains a number, but the fee can be checked. The opinion is the sentence calling the move “the best thing the city has ever done.”
items.explain: “Moving the market downtown is the best thing the city has ever done for small businesses” is an opinion: “the best thing” is a judgment people could disagree with. Every other sentence (the date, the hours, the number of sellers, the fee, the parking) can be checked.

items.prompt: Over ten winters, a state’s spending on road salt and its number of winter car accidents rose and fell together. A lawmaker concludes, “Road salt causes car accidents.” Which statement best evaluates this conclusion?
options: It is not supported, because a third factor, such as heavy snowfall, could increase both salt use and accidents.
It is supported, because salt spending and accidents moved together in every one of the ten winters.
It is supported, because road salt was spread on the roads before most of the accidents took place.
It is not supported, because ten winters is too short a time for any pattern in the data to matter.
why: Moving together every winter shows a strong correlation, not a cause. A snowy winter would raise both numbers.
Coming first is not enough to prove a cause. Salt is spread when storms arrive, and storms also cause accidents.
Ten winters can show a real pattern. The problem is not the length of time but that a third factor could explain both.
items.explain: Salt use and accidents rise together because of something they share: bad winter weather. Snowy, icy winters lead the state to spread more salt and lead to more accidents. That third factor explains the correlation without salt causing anything. The “every one of the ten winters” answer is tempting, but a consistent correlation is still only a correlation.

vocab.def: A record created by someone who took part in or witnessed an event, at or near the time it happened.
vocab.example: A letter a soldier wrote home in 1863.

vocab.def: A work that describes or interprets events after they happened, usually based on primary sources.
vocab.example: A textbook chapter about the Civil War.

vocab.def: A one-sided view that favors one position and leaves out or downplays others.
vocab.example: An article about a strike that quotes only the factory owner.

vocab.def: Information, often one-sided, spread on purpose to shape public opinion or behavior.
vocab.example: A wartime poster urging people to enlist.

vocab.def: A statement that can be proven true or false with evidence.
vocab.example: The 2020 Census counted about 331 million people in the United States.

vocab.def: A statement of belief, feeling, or judgment that cannot be proven true or false.
vocab.example: “The new bridge is the ugliest building in town.”

vocab.def: The position or perspective from which a person sees and describes events.
vocab.example: A worker and an owner describe the same strike differently.

vocab.def: A relationship in which one event (the cause) makes another event (the effect) happen.
vocab.example: A long drought led to crop failures.

vocab.def: Two things that change at the same time or in a pattern; this alone does not prove that one causes the other.
vocab.example: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer.

vocab.def: The part of a map that explains what its symbols, colors, or labels mean.
vocab.example: A star in the key stands for the county seat.

vocab.def: The part of a map that shows how distance on the map compares to real distance.
A symbol on a map that shows the directions north, south, east, and west.
vocab.example: The compass rose shows that north is at the top of the map.

vocab.def: A judgment reached by reasoning from evidence; on the GED it must be supported by the information given.
vocab.example: The table shows the population roughly doubled from 1900 to 1950.

vocab.def: Words chosen to stir strong positive or negative feelings.
vocab.example: Calling protesters “a mob” instead of “a crowd.”

vocab.def: The unit for the difference between two percents; find it by subtracting one percent from the other.
vocab.example: Turnout rising from 42% to 55% is an increase of 13 percentage points.

notes:
Week 9 Study Sheet: Social Studies Practices

Every stimulus: Who made it? When? Why? What does it actually show?

Maps

  • Find: title, north, key, scale
  • North at top: up = north, right = east
  • “Where is A from B?” Start at B, travel to A
  • Grid: compare rows (N/S), then columns (E/W), combine
  • Distance = squares moved × miles per square (do not count the start square)

Charts and Tables

  • Read title, labels, units, source first
  • Bar = compare groups; line = change over time; circle = parts of one whole (100%); table = exact values
  • Percentage points: subtract (55% − 42% = 13 points)
  • Count = percent × total (25% of $40 million = $10 million)
  • A percent is a share, not a count
  • Supported = provable from the data. Cross out causes, predictions, “all/every/always”

Fact, Opinion, Point of View

  • Fact: can be checked (true or false)
  • Opinion: judgment; should, best, worst, unfair, too high, I believe
  • A number does not make a sentence a fact
  • Point of view: where the writer stands shapes what is included and the words used

Cause and Effect

  • Signals: because, led to, as a result, so, due to
  • A cause comes before its effect; effects can become new causes (chains)
  • After ≠ because of. Correlation is not proof.
  • Test a cause: was the change already happening? Did similar places without the cause change too?
Primary sourceSecondary source
Made by a participant or witness, at the time: letters, diaries, speeches, laws, photos, posters, records, news reports from the timeMade later by someone interpreting events: textbooks, encyclopedias, documentaries, biographies, most history books
Good for: first-hand evidence; how people thought then. Caution: one creator’s view and purposeGood for: context and the big picture. Caution: the author’s interpretation
Propaganda techniqueWhat it does
Bandwagon“Everyone is doing it”
Name-callingNegative label on a person or idea
Glittering generalitiesVague feel-good words, no details
TestimonialFamous or trusted person endorses
TransferLinks idea to a respected symbol (flag, Uncle Sam)
Card stackingOnly the facts that help one side
Plain folks“I’m just like you”
FearDanger unless you act

Persuasive sources (posters, ads, speeches) are strong evidence of what their makers wanted, weak evidence of what people actually did or felt. Bias clues: loaded words, missing facts, one side quoted, a creator who gains.
